AI.tldr: This study uses equation-of-motion coupled cluster (EOM-CC) theory to analyze the vibronic and magnetic properties of $5d^2$ W sites in the correlated insulator Cs$_2$WCl$_6$. The authors derive model Hamiltonians, simulate RIXS spectra (finding asymmetric peaks due to vibronic coupling), and calculate effective magnetic moments that match experimental temperature dependence. They identify a weak Jahn-Teller regime where dynamic (not static) Jahn-Teller effects modulate RIXS spectra and magnetic moments, demonstrating EOM-CC's utility for predicting physical phenomena in correlated insulators.
AI.motivation: To quantitatively unravel the nature of $5d^2$ centers in correlated insulators, specifically the interplay among charge, spin, orbital, and lattice degrees of freedom, which remains poorly understood in cubic $5d^2$ double perovskites where no experimental evidence of symmetry-lowering in low-temperature ordered phases has been reported despite predicted Jahn-Teller activity.
AI.method: The authors apply equation-of-motion coupled cluster (EOM-CC) theory to analyze $5d^2$ W sites in Cs$_2$WCl$_6$. They derive electronic and vibronic model Hamiltonians, simulate W $L_3$ edge resonant inelastic x-ray scattering (RIXS) spectra, and calculate the effective magnetic moment.
AI.result: Simulated RIXS spectra show vibronic coupling produces asymmetric peaks. Calculated effective magnetic moments exhibit temperature dependence consistent with experimental observations, confirming the low-energy level distribution. The Jahn-Teller effect is found to be in a weak regime—no noticeable static deformation occurs, but dynamic Jahn-Teller effects modulate RIXS spectral shapes and influence the magnetic moment.
AI.conclusion: The EOM-CC method is demonstrated to be useful for predicting physical phenomena on metal sites in correlated insulating materials.

title: Entropic Necks, Dynamic Crossovers, and Fragility in Supercooled Liquids
summary: The dramatic slowdown of dynamics in supercooled liquids is accompanied by a sequence of dynamical crossovers, most notably the transition from high-temperature collision-dominated transport to low-temperature activated structural relaxation. A particularly striking manifestation of this change is the crossover from Rosenfeld excess-entropy scaling to the Adam--Gibbs relation. In this work we develop a theoretical framework based on a configuration-space extension of Zwanzig's entropic-neck picture and combine it with a Mori--Zwanzig memory-function formalism to address anomalies of supercooled liquids. The central idea is that structural relaxation is controlled by the narrowing of configurational pathways connecting metastable basins of the inherent-structure landscape. Starting from coupled slow variables describing intrabasin motion and neck fluctuations, we derive a reduced generalized Langevin description in which elimination of the neck coordinate generates a long-lived memory kernel and naturally leads to entropy-controlled activated dynamics. At high temperatures the neck is broad and readily accessible, yielding Rosenfeld-type transport governed primarily by local structural entropy. Upon cooling, progressive neck constriction produces an increasing entropy deficit, leading to Adam--Gibbs behavior and activated relaxation. Within this picture, fragility acquires a simple geometric interpretation: fragile liquids are characterized by a rapid collapse of the effective configurational neck with decreasing temperature, whereas strong liquids exhibit a much slower evolution of accessible pathways. The framework does not by itself compute the configurational entropy, mismatch penalty, or cooperative length from microscopic interactions; its aim is to provide a dynamical and geometrical interpretation.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a theoretical framework combining configuration-space Zwanzig entropic-neck picture with Mori-Zwanzig memory-function formalism to explain dynamical crossovers in supercooled liquids, particularly the transition from Rosenfeld excess-entropy scaling to Adam-Gibbs relation, attributing activated relaxation to the narrowing of configurational pathways between inherent-structure basins.
AI.motivation: To address the dramatic slowdown of dynamics in supercooled liquids and explain the sequence of dynamical crossovers, especially the transition from collision-dominated transport to activated structural relaxation and the crossover from Rosenfeld scaling to Adam-Gibbs relation.
AI.method: Combines a configuration-space extension of Zwanzig's entropic-neck picture with a Mori-Zwanzig memory-function formalism; derives a reduced generalized Langevin description from coupled slow variables (intrabasin motion and neck fluctuations), where elimination of the neck coordinate generates a long-lived memory kernel leading to entropy-controlled activated dynamics.
AI.result: At high temperatures, the broad accessible neck yields Rosenfeld-type transport governed by local structural entropy; upon cooling, progressive neck constriction produces an increasing entropy deficit, leading to Adam-Gibbs behavior and activated relaxation. Fragility acquires a geometric interpretation: fragile liquids show rapid collapse of configurational neck, strong liquids show slower evolution.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a dynamical and geometrical interpretation of supercooled liquid anomalies without computing configurational entropy, mismatch penalty, or cooperative length from microscopic interactions.

title: The limits of interpretability in multiple linear regression
summary: Interpreting machine-learning models has attracted increasing attention, particularly in the physical sciences, where one often seeks to understand the underlying mechanisms rather than merely make predictions. Multiple linear regression is often regarded as an interpretable alternative to more complex models, such as deep neural networks, because its predictions are expressed as explicit weighted sums of input features. However, when input features are strongly correlated, namely in the presence of multicollinearity, the learned weights can exhibit large dataset-to-dataset fluctuations and oscillatory behavior across physically similar features, making their interpretation difficult or even impossible. Although the instability of the weights under multicollinearity is well known in statistics, its consequences for physical interpretation, in particular its connection to oscillatory weights across physically similar features, have not been systematically clarified. Here, we theoretically discuss the mechanism behind this loss of interpretability by analyzing the eigenmodes of the feature correlation matrix. We show that small-eigenvalue modes associated with multicollinearity amplify fluctuations in the weights and generate oscillatory patterns that do not necessarily reflect meaningful contributions. We test this theoretical picture numerically on physics datasets and show that Ridge regularization suppresses these unstable modes, although the resulting weights must still be interpreted with caution. We further confirm the generality of our findings beyond physics by analyzing a diverse collection of publicly available datasets. Our results clarify why, in the presence of multicollinearity, physical interpretation can remain difficult even for linear regression models.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how multicollinearity (strong feature correlations) causes instability and oscillatory patterns in linear regression weights, undermining interpretability in physical sciences, and shows that while Ridge regularization suppresses these unstable modes, caution is still needed.
AI.motivation: Although linear regression is often considered interpretable, its weights become unstable and oscillatory under multicollinearity, yet the specific consequences for physical interpretation have not been systematically clarified.
AI.method: The authors theoretically analyze the eigenmodes of the feature correlation matrix to explain how small-eigenvalue modes amplify weight fluctuations and generate oscillatory patterns, then validate numerically on physics datasets and diverse public datasets.
AI.result: Multicollinearity-induced small-eigenvalue modes amplify weight fluctuations and create oscillatory patterns; Ridge regularization suppresses these unstable modes but still requires cautious interpretation.
AI.conclusion: Even linear regression models can suffer from interpretability difficulties under multicollinearity, and practitioners must be aware that learned weights may not reflect meaningful physical contributions.

title: Thermodynamics of 2-undecanone + n-alkane mixtures
summary: Densities and excess molar volumes ($V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$) at (293.15-303.15) K and excess molar enthalpies ($H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$) at 298.15 K are reported for 2-undecanone + heptane, or + octane, or + decane, or + dodecane, or + tetradecane mixtures at 95 kPa. Densities and $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ were measured using, respectively, a densitometer Anton Paar DMA 602 and a Tian-Calvet micro-calorimeter. $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ results are positive, indicating that interactions between like molecules are dominant. Both $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ and $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ increase in line with $n$ (number of C atoms of the alkane), which reveals that the increase of $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ can be ascribed to an increased interactional contribution. Nevertheless, systems with $n$ = 7,8 show negative $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ values, which reveals that $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ is determined mainly by structural effects. Isochoric excess molar internal energies ($U_{V\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$) at 298.15 K have been obtained from the present $H_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ and $V_{\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ data. At equimolar composition, $U_{V\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$is nearly constant for $n$ = 7-10, and then slightly increases. This has been explained in terms of a possible folding of 2-undecanone. From the comparison of $U_{V\text{m}}^{\text{E}}$ results for similar systems involving n-alkanoates, it is shown that folding is more likely in solutions with these compounds.

AI.tldr: This paper reports experimental densities, excess molar volumes (V_m^E), and excess molar enthalpies (H_m^E) for binary mixtures of 2-undecanone with various alkanes (heptane to tetradecane). H_m^E is positive and increases with alkane chain length; V_m^E also increases with chain length but is negative for shorter alkanes (n=7,8), attributed to structural effects. Isochoric excess molar internal energies (U_Vm^E) are derived and indicate possible folding of 2-undecanone, more likely than in analogous n-alkanoate systems.
AI.motivation: To understand the thermodynamic behavior and molecular interactions in binary mixtures of 2-undecanone with n-alkanes of varying chain length, and to investigate structural vs. interactional contributions to excess properties.
AI.method: Densities measured with Anton Paar DMA 602 densitometer; excess molar enthalpies measured with Tian-Calvet micro-calorimeter at 95 kPa. Excess molar volumes and isochoric excess molar internal energies derived from experimental data.
AI.result: H_m^E positive for all mixtures, increasing with alkane chain length. V_m^E negative for n=7,8 but increases with n; U_Vm^E nearly constant at equimolar composition for n=7-10, then slightly increases.
AI.conclusion: Interactions between like molecules dominate (positive H_m^E). V_m^E is governed by structural effects for short-chain alkanes and interactional contributions for longer chains. Folding of 2-undecanone is more likely in these solutions compared to n-alkanoate mixtures.

title: Absence of orbital current torque in a magnetic metal/Pt/CuOx trilayer
summary: Naturally oxidized copper (CuOx) was cited as an exceptionally strong orbital-current source despite the keen debate over the concept of orbital current. Here, we report unambiguous experimental evidence for the absence of a detectable orbital-current torque in the Fe/Pt/CuOx trilayers. Using a magnetic metal detector of Fe thin film with a negligible self-induced torque, the damping-like torque due to Pt/CuOx bilayers is clarified to entirely arise from the spin Hall spin current of the Pt. As the Pt thickness increases, the torque for Fe/Pt/CuOx and Fe/Pt/MgO increases coherently and monotonically, as exactly expected from the spin Hall effect of Pt and the drift-diffusion model of spin angular momentum. These findings suggest poor generality or even universal absence of orbital current torque.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that the damping-like torque previously attributed to orbital currents from naturally oxidized copper (CuOx) actually originates entirely from the spin Hall effect of platinum (Pt), disproving claims of orbital-current torque in Fe/Pt/CuOx trilayers.
AI.motivation: To resolve the debated existence of orbital current torque and test whether CuOx is truly an exceptionally strong orbital-current source, as previously claimed.
AI.method: Using Fe thin film as a magnetic metal detector with negligible self-induced torque, the authors measured damping-like torque in Fe/Pt/CuOx and Fe/Pt/MgO trilayers as a function of Pt thickness, comparing results against spin Hall effect and drift-diffusion model predictions.
AI.result: No detectable orbital-current torque was found; the torque in Pt/CuOx bilayers arises entirely from the spin Hall spin current of Pt. Torque increased coherently and monotonically with Pt thickness, exactly matching spin Hall effect and drift-diffusion model expectations.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest poor generality or even universal absence of orbital current torque, contradicting earlier claims of CuOx being a strong orbital-current source.

title: Valley Valves at Domain Walls in Symmetry-Broken Rhombohedral Graphene
comment: Comments are very appreciated; 7 + 37 pages, 5 + 18 figures
summary: Rhombohedral multilayer graphene polarized by a moderate perpendicular displacement field hosts a time-reversal-symmetry-breaking valley-and-spin-polarized metallic phase that may condense into a chiral superconductor. Recent magnetic imaging and transport measurements in this unconventional system suggest the presence of domain walls both in the metallic and superconducting phases. In this work, we show that valley domain walls are impenetrable barriers to transport in the metallic regime. Transmission through such a domain wall must therefore be mediated by intervalley interactions. We derive the symmetry-allowed terms and show via microscopic numerical simulations that they enable the transmission of electrons across the domain wall. In the superconducting phase, we find that intervalley mixing is crucial for supporting an appreciable supercurrent through a SNS' Josephson junction that connects opposite-chirality superconducting regions. Taken together, our work elucidates the nature of domain walls in these experimentally relevant multilayer systems and emphasizes the critical role of intervalley hybridization plays in governing their transport properties.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how valley domain walls in rhombohedral multilayer graphene affect transport in both metallic and superconducting phases, showing that intervalley interactions are essential for transmission across these domain walls and for supporting supercurrents in Josephson junctions.
AI.motivation: Recent experiments in rhombohedral multilayer graphene suggest the presence of domain walls in both metallic and superconducting phases, but their transport properties are poorly understood.
AI.method: The authors derive symmetry-allowed intervalley interaction terms and perform microscopic numerical simulations to study electron transmission across valley domain walls.
AI.result: Valley domain walls act as impenetrable barriers to transport in the metallic regime unless mediated by intervalley interactions. In the superconducting phase, intervalley mixing is crucial for supporting appreciable supercurrents through SNS' Josephson junctions connecting opposite-chirality superconducting regions.
AI.conclusion: Intervalley hybridization plays a critical role in governing the transport properties of domain walls in rhombohedral multilayer graphene systems.

title: Cluster-based Message-Passing (CluMP) Optimization for Complex QUBO Problems
summary:
Quadratic Unconstrained Boolean Optimization (QUBO) problems are widespread in both industrial applications and scientific studies. A QUBO problem corresponds to the optimization of a system of Ising spins defined on a generally sparse and heterogeneous graph. When the QUBO problem contains conflicting requests, the corresponding Ising system is frustrated, generating a complex energy landscape, which is hard to explore and optimize. Despite extensive algorithmic and hardware developments, finding low-energy configurations in these systems remains challenging (e.g., local-update heuristics typically become trapped in metastable states), especially when the (possibly frustrated) interactions generate extended correlated domains.
  We introduce CluMP (Cluster-based Message-Passing), an algorithm that performs collective updates on connected clusters of spins using information from Belief Propagation (BP). By controlling the amount of frustration within clusters, CluMP enables BP convergence on large subgraphs and proposes nonlocal rearrangements involving up to hundreds of spins in a single move. We benchmark CluMP against state-of-the-art local-update heuristics on spin-glass models defined on several graph topologies, including random regular graphs and lattice regular graphs in two and three dimensions. Cluster moves consistently bypass local trapping and reach lower energies with fewer effective operations than single-spin dynamics. These results demonstrate that frustration-tolerant cluster updates can be implemented efficiently on sparse graphs. The CluMP framework provides a scalable strategy for large-scale combinatorial optimization and inference problems, where exploiting medium- and long-range correlations is key to navigating complex energy landscapes.

AI.tldr: CluMP is a cluster-based message-passing algorithm that uses Belief Propagation to perform collective updates on connected spin clusters in QUBO/Ising problems, achieving lower energies and escaping metastable states more efficiently than local-update heuristics on sparse graphs.
AI.motivation: QUBO problems (Ising spin systems on sparse heterogeneous graphs) often suffer from frustration, which creates complex energy landscapes where local-update heuristics become trapped in metastable states, especially when frustration generates extended correlated domains.
AI.method: CluMP (Cluster-based Message-Passing) performs collective updates on connected clusters of spins using Belief Propagation (BP). It controls the amount of frustration within clusters to enable BP convergence on large subgraphs, proposing nonlocal rearrangements involving up to hundreds of spins per move.
AI.result: Benchmarked against state-of-the-art local-update heuristics on spin-glass models across multiple graph topologies (random regular graphs, 2D and 3D lattice regular graphs), CluMP consistently bypasses local trapping and reaches lower energies with fewer effective operations than single-spin dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Frustration-tolerant cluster updates can be implemented efficiently on sparse graphs, and CluMP provides a scalable strategy for large-scale combinatorial optimization and inference problems where exploiting medium- to long-range correlations is key.

title: Non-stationary longitudinal Josephson effect in electron-hole bilayers
summary: The non-stationary longitudinal Josephson effect in bilayer systems with pairing of spatially separated electrons and holes is investigated. The tunneling current between two (right and left) weakly coupled electron-hole condensates is analyzed in the presence of an external voltage applied along the layers. Two limiting regimes are considered: the high-density regime, where pairing occurs in momentum space similarly to conventional superconductors, and the low-density regime corresponding to a Bose-Einstein condensate of spatially indirect excitons. Using the tunneling Hamiltonian approach, expressions for the quasiparticle, superconducting and interference contributions to the tunneling current are derived. It is shown that in the high-density limit the quasiparticle and interference currents vanish at zero temperature below a threshold voltage determined by the energy gap, so that only the supercurrent remains. In contrast, in the low-density regime the gapless spectrum of collective excitations leads to finite dissipative contributions even at zero temperature, resulting in damping of Josephson oscillations. For spatially separated tunneling barriers with distance exceeding the coherence length, phase jumps occur at each barrier, resulting in voltage oscillations across the electron and hole barriers and a non-sinusoidal current-phase relation governed by the critical currents of the two barriers.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the non-stationary longitudinal Josephson effect in bilayer electron-hole systems, deriving tunneling current expressions using the tunneling Hamiltonian approach. In the high-density (BCS-like) regime, quasiparticle and interference currents vanish below a threshold voltage at zero temperature, leaving only supercurrent. In the low-density (BEC-like) regime, a gapless spectrum leads to finite dissipation and damping. For separated tunneling barriers beyond the coherence length, phase jumps occur, producing voltage oscillations and a non-sinusoidal current-phase relation.
AI.motivation: To understand how longitudinal Josephson tunneling behaves in bilayer systems with electron-hole pairing under non-stationary conditions, particularly across different density regimes and spatially separated barriers.
AI.method: The tunneling Hamiltonian approach is employed to analyze tunneling current between weakly coupled electron-hole condensates under an external voltage. Two regimes are considered: high-density (momentum-space pairing, BCS-like) and low-density (Bose-Einstein condensate of indirect excitons).
AI.result: In the high-density limit, quasiparticle and interference currents vanish at zero temperature below a threshold voltage (set by the energy gap), leaving only supercurrent. In the low-density regime, the gapless collective excitation spectrum yields finite dissipative contributions even at zero temperature, damping Josephson oscillations. For spatially separated barriers beyond the coherence length, phase jumps at each barrier induce voltage oscillations and a non-sinusoidal current-phase relation determined by critical currents of each barrier.
AI.conclusion: The non-stationary Josephson effect in electron-hole bilayers exhibits qualitatively different behavior depending on density: dissipationless supercurrent in the high-density BCS regime, and damped oscillations with dissipation in the low-density BEC regime. Spatial separation of tunneling barriers introduces additional complexity via phase jumps and non-sinusoidal current-phase relationships.

title: Contrastive learning of dynamical representations for enhanced molecular sampling
summary: Identifying collective variables that capture slow dynamical modes is essential for sampling rare events in complex systems. Existing machine-learning approaches often require predefined metastable states, carefully chosen descriptors, or training trajectories with high-quality kinetic information. Here, we introduce SelfTICA, a self-supervised contrastive-learning framework that reformulates collective-variable discovery as dynamical representation learning. SelfTICA defines positive and negative pairs from time-lagged molecular configurations, learns reusable features through a contrastive objective linked to spectral variational principles, and extracts orthogonal slow modes by applying time-lagged independent component analysis in the learned representation space. By decoupling representation learning from slow-mode extraction, SelfTICA avoids direct optimization of eigendecomposition-based objectives and enables spectra and collective variables to be evaluated across lag times without retraining. Across different atomistic systems, SelfTICA learns dynamical representations from limited, biased, or exploratory data and converts them into collective variables that accelerate rare-event exploration and improve free-energy convergence.

AI.tldr: SelfTICA is a self-supervised contrastive-learning framework that discovers collective variables (slow dynamical modes) from molecular dynamics data by learning dynamical representations via time-lagged contrastive learning and then applying TICA in the learned space, enabling efficient rare-event sampling without predefined states or extensive training data.
AI.motivation: Existing machine-learning approaches for discovering collective variables often require predefined metastable states, carefully chosen descriptors, or high-quality training trajectories with kinetic information, limiting their applicability.
AI.method: SelfTICA uses a self-supervised contrastive-learning framework that defines positive/negative pairs from time-lagged molecular configurations, learns features via a contrastive objective linked to spectral variational principles, and extracts orthogonal slow modes using TICA in the learned representation space. This decouples representation learning from slow-mode extraction, avoiding direct eigendecomposition optimization.
AI.result: Across different atomistic systems, SelfTICA learns dynamical representations from limited, biased, or exploratory data and converts them into collective variables that accelerate rare-event exploration and improve free-energy convergence.
AI.conclusion: SelfTICA provides a flexible framework for collective-variable discovery that is robust to data limitations and enables evaluation of spectra and collective variables across lag times without retraining.

title: Stabilizing Itinerant Electrons in a Corner-Sharing Kagomé Oxide Nd4Os3ZnO14
summary: Kagome oxides provide a fertile platform for exploring exotic electronic states arising from geometrical frustration and characteristic band topology. Here, we report the synthesis of a 5d transition-metal kagome oxide, Nd4Os3ZnO14, obtained via high-temperature, high-pressure hydrothermal synthesis. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction reveals a two-dimensional kagome network formed by corner-sharing OsO6 octahedra, with a nominal osmium valence of +4.67. In-plane resistivity and hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy measurements indicate that the semimetallic electronic structure at room temperature evolves into a semiconducting ground state upon cooling, accompanied by a pronounced enhancement of hole mobility. Magnetic susceptibility measurements demonstrate localized Nd3+ moments without long-range magnetic order down to 2 K. The coexistence of a metallic kagome plane, strong spin-orbit coupling inherent to 5d electrons, and rare-earth magnetism establishes Nd4Os3ZnO14 as a promising platform for investigating correlated electron phenomena in kagome oxides within the itinerant regime.

AI.tldr: The paper reports the synthesis and characterization of a new 5d transition-metal kagome oxide, Nd4Os3ZnO14, which exhibits a semimetal-to-semiconductor transition upon cooling, enhanced hole mobility, localized Nd3+ moments without long-range magnetic order, and serves as a promising platform for studying correlated electron phenomena in kagome oxides.
AI.motivation: To explore exotic electronic states in kagome oxides by extending the family to 5d transition-metal systems, where strong spin-orbit coupling and geometrical frustration can produce novel correlated electron phenomena.
AI.method: High-temperature, high-pressure hydrothermal synthesis; single-crystal X-ray diffraction for structural determination; in-plane resistivity and hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy for electronic characterization; magnetic susceptibility measurements.
AI.result: A two-dimensional kagome network of corner-sharing OsO6 octahedra with nominal Os valence of +4.67; semimetallic electronic structure at room temperature evolves into semiconducting ground state upon cooling with enhanced hole mobility; localized Nd3+ moments with no long-range magnetic order down to 2 K.
AI.conclusion: Nd4Os3ZnO14 is a promising platform for investigating correlated electron phenomena in kagome oxides, combining a metallic kagome plane, strong 5d spin-orbit coupling, and rare-earth magnetism in the itinerant regime.

title: Self-Consistent Closure of Fractal Dimension, Nonextensive Statistics, and Non-Markovian Dynamics in Critical Systems
summary: Self-organized critical systems often exhibit three macroscopic features simultaneously: nonextensive thermodynamics (quantified by the Tsallis index $q$), structural fractality (measured by the Hausdorff dimension $D$), and non-Markovian dynamics (characterized by the memory exponent $α$). Historically, these parameters have been treated as independent, to be empirically fitted case by case. Here we demonstrate that phase-space self-consistency imposes a unique algebraic closure: $α=D/(2D-1)$. This relation, together with $q=1+1/D$ derived from the extensivity of Tsallis entropy on fractal supports, yields the known result $α=1/(3-q)$ as a consequence, not as an independent assumption. The closure contains no free parameters and satisfies the physical boundary conditions $α(1)=1$ (ballistic transport in Euclidean spaces) and $α\to1/2$ as $D\to\infty$ (maximally subdiffusive regime). We validate the Troika relation across eight independent experimental systems, including seismicity, electromagnetic precursors, EEG, urban networks, botanical architectures, and space plasma. All measured values fall within error bars of the theoretical prediction, establishing the universality of the closure.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a universal algebraic closure relation α = D/(2D-1) linking self-organized critical systems' memory exponent (α), Hausdorff dimension (D), and Tsallis index (q), validated across eight diverse experimental systems with no free parameters.
AI.motivation: Historically, the three macroscopic features of self-organized critical systems—nonextensive thermodynamics (q), structural fractality (D), and non-Markovian dynamics (α)—have been treated as independent parameters requiring empirical fitting case by case, lacking a unified theoretical framework.
AI.method: Phase-space self-consistency is used to derive the algebraic closure α = D/(2D-1). Combining this with q = 1+1/D (from Tsallis entropy extensivity on fractal supports) yields α = 1/(3-q). The relation is validated against eight independent experimental systems: seismicity, electromagnetic precursors, EEG, urban networks, botanical architectures, and space plasma.
AI.result: The derived closure contains no free parameters, satisfies boundary conditions α(1)=1 (ballistic transport in Euclidean spaces) and α→1/2 as D→∞ (maximally subdiffusive regime). All measured values from eight experimental systems fall within error bars of the theoretical prediction, confirming universality.
AI.conclusion: The Troika relation establishes a universal, parameter-free closure among the three key parameters of self-organized critical systems, unifying nonextensive thermodynamics, fractality, and memory dynamics under a single theoretical framework.

title: Atomistic insights into the structural, thermal, and mechanical evolution of $Zr_{47.5}Cu_{47.5}Ag_{5}$ bulk metallic glass
summary: Bulk metallic glasses (BMGs) are distinguished by amorphous atomic structures that confer superior mechanical performance; however, the evolution of these properties in ternary bulk configurations remains insufficiently explored. In this study, we employed large-scale molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the structural, thermal, and mechanical properties of $Zr_{47.5}Cu_{47.5}Ag_{5}$ BMGs. Our thermodynamic and topological analyses, utilizing potential energy regression and the Modified Wendt-Abraham parameter, identified a glass transition temperature ($T_g$) of approximately $692\text{ K}$. Structural characterization via Voronoi tessellation and partial radial distribution functions reveals that the amorphous matrix is stabilized by icosahedral clusters, with Ag atoms inducing significant chemical heterogeneity through localized nano-clustering. Thermal transport properties, computed via the Green-Kubo formalism, demonstrate a monotonic decrease in conductivity with temperature, consistent with structural scattering saturation in disordered lattices. Mechanical tensile testing reveals that the material exhibits robust rate- and temperature-dependent behavior, with yield strengths reaching $\approx 2.3\text{ GPa}$ at room temperature. We show that macroscopic strain-softening is intrinsically linked to the thermally induced collapse of rigid icosahedral motifs, which facilitates shear band percolation. These findings provide a structural rationale for the beneficial role of Ag dopants in enhancing the resilience of multicomponent metallic glasses.

AI.tldr: This study uses molecular dynamics simulations to investigate the structural, thermal, and mechanical properties of Zr47.5Cu47.5Ag5 bulk metallic glasses, revealing a glass transition temperature of ~692 K, stabilization by icosahedral clusters, Ag-induced chemical heterogeneity, decreasing thermal conductivity with temperature, and yield strengths up to ~2.3 GPa with strain-softening linked to icosahedral motif collapse and shear band formation.
AI.motivation: The evolution of mechanical properties in ternary bulk metallic glasses remains insufficiently explored, motivating this investigation into ZrCuAg BMGs.
AI.method: Large-scale molecular dynamics simulations were employed, combined with thermodynamic analysis (potential energy regression, Modified Wendt-Abraham parameter), structural characterization (Voronoi tessellation, partial radial distribution functions), thermal transport calculations (Green-Kubo formalism), and mechanical tensile testing.
AI.result: Tg ≈ 692 K; amorphous matrix stabilized by icosahedral clusters; Ag induces chemical heterogeneity via nano-clustering; thermal conductivity decreases monotonically with temperature; yield strength reaches ~2.3 GPa at room temperature; strain-softening linked to collapse of icosahedral motifs and shear band percolation.
AI.conclusion: Ag dopants beneficially enhance the resilience of multicomponent metallic glasses, and thermally induced icosahedral motif collapse is the structural origin of macroscopic strain-softening.

title: Oxidation-induced ultrafast spin-to-orbital conversion at heavy-metal interfaces
summary: Oxidation engineering provides a route to control orbital degrees of freedom, yet its role in spin-to-orbital conversion remains largely unexplored. Here, we report an efficient spin-to-orbital conversion mechanism driven by interfacial oxidation at heavy-metal interfaces. In W/Co/SiO2 heterostructures, terahertz emission exhibits a time delay that scales linearly with the W thickness, identifying orbital-current transport as the dominant origin. The emission amplitude is approximately three times larger than that of Co/Pt bilayers, indicating highly efficient conversion from spin to orbital angular momentum. Systematic variation of Co thickness, stoichiometry, and interface configuration reveals that the effect originates from oxidation of the W layer at the W/Co interface, which modulates the interfacial orbital texture. We further show that this mechanism is generic across different heavy metals and scales with their spin-orbit coupling strength. These results establish oxidation as an effective handle to engineer spin-to-orbital conversion and provide a general route toward orbitronic terahertz emitters.

AI.tldr: Oxidation at heavy-metal interfaces enables efficient spin-to-orbital conversion, demonstrated in W/Co/SiO2 heterostructures where terahertz emission shows orbital-current transport with three times higher efficiency than Co/Pt bilayers, establishing oxidation as a general engineering tool for orbitronic terahertz emitters.
AI.motivation: Oxidation engineering can control orbital degrees of freedom, but its role in spin-to-orbital conversion has not been explored.
AI.method: Terahertz emission measurements on W/Co/SiO2 heterostructures with systematic variation of W thickness, Co thickness, stoichiometry, and interface configuration.
AI.result: Terahertz emission shows a time delay scaling linearly with W thickness (identifying orbital-current transport), emission amplitude ~3× larger than Co/Pt bilayers, and the effect originates from W oxidation at the W/Co interface modulating interfacial orbital texture; mechanism is generic across different heavy metals and scales with spin-orbit coupling strength.
AI.conclusion: Oxidation is an effective handle to engineer spin-to-orbital conversion, providing a general route toward orbitronic terahertz emitters.

title: Machine Learning Topological Order from Defect Partition Functions
summary: We introduce a machine learning framework for extracting Ising topological order from defect partition functions of the two-dimensional Ising model on a torus. Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) are trained on Ising model data sampled at criticality across topological sectors. We take a component-wise square-root map of the learned distributions which naturally produces candidate wavefunctions for the (2+1)-dimensional Ising TQFT. As a nontrivial consistency check, we extract the modular S-matrix from overlaps of the resulting states and recover the expected Ising modular data. Our results demonstrate that neural network representations can capture both critical fluctuations and emergent topological structure, providing a data-driven route from lattice statistical mechanics to topological quantum field theory.

AI.tldr: A machine learning framework uses Restricted Boltzmann Machines trained on Ising model data at criticality to extract Ising topological order, producing candidate wavefunctions for (2+1)D Ising TQFT and recovering the expected modular S-matrix.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate a data-driven method for extracting topological quantum field theory (TQFT) data directly from lattice statistical mechanics, bridging critical phenomena and topological order using neural network representations.
AI.method: Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) are trained on Ising model data sampled at criticality across topological sectors on a torus, then a component-wise square-root map is applied to the learned distributions to produce candidate wavefunctions for the (2+1)D Ising TQFT.
AI.result: The modular S-matrix extracted from overlaps of the resulting states recovers the expected Ising modular data, confirming that the learned representations capture both critical fluctuations and emergent topological structure.
AI.conclusion: Neural network representations can extract topological order from classical statistical mechanics, providing a data-driven route from lattice models to topological quantum field theory.

title: Vortex-core size and quantum geometry in flat-band superconductors
summary: We investigate the real-space vortex structure of a flat-band superconductor described by the attractive Hubbard model on the Mielke checkerboard lattice. Using a momentum-space mean-field analysis, we derive a closed-form expression for the coherence length in terms of the quantum metric of the Bloch states and a particle-hole-symmetric pair density. Self-consistent Bogoliubov-de Gennes calculations on a finite disk confirm this prediction across a wide range of fillings and interaction strengths. The coherence length is minimized at half filling, diverges toward both band edges as the pair density vanishes, and depends only logarithmically on the interaction strength. These features differ qualitatively from the conventional BCS picture, which relies on a well-defined Fermi surface and a kinetic mechanism for pair transport. Instead, the vortex-core size is governed by a geometric pair mass arising from virtual interband processes encoded in the quantum metric. Our results establish the vortex core as a direct real-space manifestation of flat-band quantum geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates vortex structures in flat-band superconductors, showing that the coherence length is governed by the quantum metric rather than BCS theory, with the vortex core serving as a real-space signature of flat-band quantum geometry.
AI.motivation: To understand the real-space vortex structure in flat-band superconductors and how the coherence length relates to quantum geometry, as conventional BCS theory fails due to the absence of a well-defined Fermi surface and kinetic pair transport mechanism.
AI.method: Momentum-space mean-field analysis to derive a closed-form expression for coherence length in terms of quantum metric and pair density; self-consistent Bogoliubov-de Gennes calculations on a finite disk for verification.
AI.result: Coherence length is minimized at half filling, diverges toward band edges as pair density vanishes, depends only logarithmically on interaction strength; governed by geometric pair mass from virtual interband processes encoded in the quantum metric.
AI.conclusion: The vortex core is a direct real-space manifestation of flat-band quantum geometry, differing qualitatively from the conventional BCS picture.

title: Liquid Random Feature Methods for Time-Dependent Partial Differential Equations
summary: A central challenge in mesh-free space--time approximation for time-dependent partial differential equations is to represent evolving temporal scales while keeping residual minimization computationally tractable. Random feature methods simplify this algebraic problem by freezing nonlinear trial functions and fitting only a linear readout, but standard static space--time activations provide no explicit relaxation-scale mechanism, making temporal-scale resolution a finite-dimensional bottleneck in stiff, dispersive, or multi-scale regimes. We introduce liquid random feature methods (L-RFM), which replace static temporal activations by closed-form liquid time-constant responses with sampled relaxation scales. The resulting frozen features form temporally structured local or global trial spaces with analytic space--time derivatives for residual least-squares assembly. A density theorem proves density of the deterministic trial spaces in the continuous space--time function class, and a temporal-rank calculation clarifies the role of sampled relaxation scales. Ablation and finite-feature tests identify the liquid temporal response as the primary source of the observed accuracy improvement. Across stiff reaction--diffusion, nonlinear transport, dispersive, complex-valued, and multidimensional benchmarks, L-RFM improves finite-feature accuracy in regimes where temporal-scale representation controls the approximation. By embedding relaxation scales directly into frozen trial functions, L-RFM provides a route to high-accuracy continuous space--time surrogates for evolutionary PDEs while preserving the simplicity of linear least-squares solvers.

AI.tldr: Liquid random feature methods (L-RFM) improve mesh-free space-time PDE approximation by replacing static temporal activations with closed-form liquid time-constant responses containing sampled relaxation scales, enabling better temporal-scale resolution while preserving linear least-squares solver simplicity.
AI.motivation: Standard random feature methods for time-dependent PDEs use static space-time activations that lack explicit relaxation-scale mechanisms, creating a finite-dimensional bottleneck for temporal-scale resolution in stiff, dispersive, or multi-scale regimes.
AI.method: L-RFM replaces static temporal activations with closed-form liquid time-constant responses incorporating sampled relaxation scales, forming temporally structured frozen trial spaces with analytic space-time derivatives for residual least-squares assembly.
AI.result: A density theorem proves trial space density in continuous space-time function class; temporal-rank calculation clarifies relaxation scale roles; ablation tests identify liquid temporal response as primary source of accuracy improvement; L-RFM outperforms across stiff reaction-diffusion, nonlinear transport, dispersive, complex-valued, and multidimensional benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: By embedding relaxation scales directly into frozen trial functions, L-RFM enables high-accuracy continuous space-time surrogates for evolutionary PDEs while maintaining the simplicity of linear least-squares solvers.

title: Probing Interfacial Magnetic Anisotropy in \texorpdfstring{CoV$_{2}$O$_{4}$}{CoV2O4} using Spin Hall Magnetoresistance
summary: Spin Hall magnetoresistance (SMR) has emerged as a powerful probe for investigating interfacial spin transport and magnetic anisotropy in complex oxide heterostructures. In this work, we investigate the interfacial magnetic anisotropy in Pt/CVO through angle-dependent magnetotransport measurements. Unlike the bulk-sensitive magnetic measurements on both strained CVO and Pt/CVO films, which exhibit a ferrimagnetic transition at $T_{C} \approx 150$ K accompanied by out-of-plane anisotropy that reorients toward in-plane anisotropy below 90 K, SMR reveals a distinct interfacial magnetic anisotropy. The rotational scans of the in-plane transverse SMR at 20 K exhibit substantial hysteresis about [100], while no hysteresis is observed along [110] and [1$\bar{1}$0], indicating a biaxial anisotropy with easy axes along [110] and [1$\bar{1}$0]. Furthermore, the absence of sharp discontinuities in both the in-plane longitudinal and transverse SMR, together with pronounced discontinuities near the in-plane [010] direction during out-of-plane rotation, strongly indicates the presence of in-plane anisotropy. This behavior persists up to 120 K. The discrepancy between the bulk-sensitive magnetic measurements and the SMR response suggests that the Pt/CVO interface retains a magnetic anisotropy distinct from the bulk, highlighting the interfacial sensitivity of SMR. Additionally, the spin mixing conductance is found to be of the order of $10^{14}$ $Ω^{-1}\mathrm{m}^{-2}$, comparable to other oxide-based spintronic systems. These findings highlight the crucial role of interfacial effects in spin transport and establish Pt/CVO as a promising platform for spintronic applications.

AI.tldr: Using spin Hall magnetoresistance (SMR), the study reveals that Pt/CVO heterostructures exhibit a distinct interfacial biaxial magnetic anisotropy (easy axes along [110] and [1$\bar{1}$0]) that differs from the bulk ferrimagnetic anisotropy, with spin mixing conductance ~10^{14} Ω^{-1}m^{-2}, highlighting interfacial sensitivity for oxide spintronics.
AI.motivation: To uncover the interfacial magnetic anisotropy in Pt/CVO heterostructures, which cannot be resolved by bulk-sensitive magnetic measurements but is critical for understanding spin transport in oxide-based spintronic systems.
AI.method: Angle-dependent magnetotransport measurements, specifically in-plane and out-of-plane rotational scans of longitudinal and transverse spin Hall magnetoresistance (SMR), were performed on Pt/CVO films at cryogenic temperatures (20 K–120 K).
AI.result: In-plane transverse SMR at 20 K shows hysteresis about [100] but not along [110] and [1$\bar{1}$0], indicating biaxial anisotropy with easy axes along [110] and [1$\bar{1}$0]. No sharp discontinuities appear in in-plane scans, but out-of-plane rotations show discontinuities near [010], confirming in-plane anisotropy persisting up to 120 K. Spin mixing conductance is ~10^{14} Ω^{-1}m^{-2}.
AI.conclusion: The Pt/CVO interface retains a distinct magnetic anisotropy differing from the bulk, demonstrating the interfacial sensitivity of SMR and establishing Pt/CVO as a promising platform for spintronic applications.

title: Complementary Thermodynamic Mechanisms of Boron and Carbon Segregation at Grain Boundaries in Nickel Alloys
summary: Grain boundary stabilization by light interstitials is central to the performance of Ni-based superalloys, yet the thermodynamic mechanisms governing their interactions with substitutional chemistry remain poorly resolved. Here, we use hybrid Monte Carlo molecular dynamics simulations to quantify how boron and carbon modify the thermodynamic, structural, and chemical ordering of grain boundaries in Ni--Cr alloys. By analyzing interfacial state variables, site-resolved segregation spectra, local chemical ordering, and structural evolution, we show that boron and carbon stabilize grain boundaries through complementary pathways. Carbon drives saturation-controlled stabilization by recruiting Cr and conditioning boundary chemistry, while suppressing temperature-driven structural transformations of the boundary. In contrast, boron stabilizes grain boundaries through a selective mechanism that lowers the interfacial grand potential via localized ordering while permitting gradual structural evolution. These effects arise from coupled interactions between interstitial segregation and Cr redistribution, which together regulate site accessibility, chemical competition, and the range of accessible interfacial states. This work provides a thermodynamic framework for grain boundary engineering and suggests design principles for leveraging interstitial-substitutional interactions in alloys.

AI.tldr: Using hybrid Monte Carlo molecular dynamics simulations, this study reveals that carbon and boron stabilize grain boundaries in Ni-Cr alloys through distinct complementary mechanisms—carbon via saturation-controlled Cr recruitment and structural suppression, boron via selective interfacial grand potential reduction with gradual structural evolution—establishing a thermodynamic framework for grain boundary engineering.
AI.motivation: The thermodynamic mechanisms governing interactions between light interstitials (e.g., B, C) and substitutional chemistry at grain boundaries in Ni-based superalloys remain poorly resolved, despite the central role of interstitial stabilization in alloy performance.
AI.method: Hybrid Monte Carlo molecular dynamics simulations were employed to quantify how boron and carbon modify thermodynamic, structural, and chemical ordering of grain boundaries in Ni-Cr alloys, analyzing interfacial state variables, site-resolved segregation spectra, local chemical ordering, and structural evolution.
AI.result: Carbon stabilizes boundaries via saturation-controlled Cr recruitment and chemical conditioning while suppressing temperature-driven structural transformations; boron stabilizes boundaries through selective lowering of interfacial grand potential via localized ordering while allowing gradual structural evolution. Both effects arise from coupled interstitial segregation and Cr redistribution.
AI.conclusion: This work provides a thermodynamic framework for grain boundary engineering and suggests design principles leveraging interstitial-substitutional interactions in alloys.

title: High-sensitivity hydrogen gas permeation: system development, sample preparation, and influence of testing variables
summary: There is a need to develop quantitative, high-resolution hydrogen gas (H2) permeation techniques to provide a better understanding of hydrogen-material interactions. This study aims to develop and validate a high-sensitivity H2 permeation system, which is then leveraged to systematically quantify the influence of surface condition and key testing variables (surface oxides, residual gas impurities, pressure, and temperature) on hydrogen permeation. A gas permeation system capable of operating at pressures up to 50 bar and temperatures up to 250 C was developed, incorporating high-sensitivity mass spectrometric detection and controlled surface preparation protocols. Permeation transients were analysed in a model material (annealed pure Fe) to determine hydrogen diffusivity and permeability under systematically varied surface states, oxygen contents, pressures and temperatures. Surface oxides are shown to play a dominant role in controlling hydrogen permeation at room temperature. The presence of oxide layers can severely hinder or completely suppress hydrogen uptake, with measurable permeation requiring oxide removal via pickling and Pd coating on both surfaces, or activation through hydrogen-assisted reduction at elevated temperature. Residual oxygen present prior to hydrogen exposure further reduces permeability by modifying surface boundary conditions, indicating strongly surface-controlled kinetics. Under optimised surface conditions, hydrogen transport follows bulk diffusion-controlled behaviour, with steady-state flux obeying Sieverts' law at 25 C (1-5 bar) and diffusivity and permeability exhibiting Arrhenius behaviour between 25 and 150 C at 5 bar, indicating bulk diffusion-controlled transport. The developed system resolves hydrogen fluxes as low as 1.98x10-9 mol(m2 s) and provides a robust platform for investigating surface, mechanical and environmental effects on H2 permeation.

AI.tldr: This study develops a high-sensitivity H₂ permeation system (up to 50 bar, 250°C) and systematically quantifies how surface oxides, oxygen impurities, pressure, and temperature affect hydrogen permeation in annealed pure Fe. Surface oxides dominate at room temperature and can block permeation entirely; removal via pickling, Pd coating, or high-temperature hydrogen-assisted reduction is required. Under optimized conditions, transport follows bulk-diffusion-controlled Sieverts' law and Arrhenius behavior. The system achieves a detection limit of 1.98×10⁻⁹ mol/(m²·s).
AI.motivation: There is a need to develop quantitative, high-resolution hydrogen gas (H₂) permeation techniques to better understand hydrogen-material interactions.
AI.method: A gas permeation system operating up to 50 bar and 250°C was built with high-sensitivity mass spectrometry and controlled surface preparation (pickling, Pd coating). Permeation transients were measured in annealed pure Fe under systematically varied surface states, oxygen contents, pressures, and temperatures.
AI.result: Surface oxides dominate permeation at room temperature, often completely suppressing H₂ uptake. Residual oxygen reduces permeability. After optimal surface preparation, transport follows bulk-diffusion-controlled behavior: Sieverts' law at 25°C (1–5 bar) and Arrhenius behavior at 25–150°C (5 bar). Minimum detectable flux is 1.98×10⁻⁹ mol/(m²·s).
AI.conclusion: The developed system provides a robust platform for investigating surface, mechanical, and environmental effects on H₂ permeation, with surface condition being the critical controlling factor at low temperatures.

title: Precipitation strengthening: a collective multi-dislocation phenomenon
summary: Precipitation strengthening is a cornerstone of physical metallurgy, delivering otherwise unattainable combinations of strength and ductility. The approach relies on nanoscale precipitates that impede the motion of dislocations, the primary carriers of plastic deformation. Historically, precipitation strengthening has been rationalized via two idealized, limiting mechanisms: dislocations either cut through or bow around precipitates. However, in situ experiments cannot yet resolve the coupled, real-time evolution of dislocation networks and nanoprecipitates, leaving these atomic-scale dynamics inaccessible to direct observation. Here, using large-scale atomistic simulations that fully capture these dynamics, we demonstrate that the classical cutting-versus-bowing dichotomy is incomplete. Instead, strengthening arises as an emergent collective phenomenon driven by concurrent, multi-dislocation interactions. These interactions simultaneously induce dislocation accumulation at interfaces, storage within precipitates, and precipitate-mediated multiplication inside the matrix. These findings establish a mechanistic framework that transcends traditional models and provides a new foundation for predicting strengthening behavior.

AI.tldr: Using large-scale atomistic simulations, this paper shows that precipitation strengthening is not simply explained by dislocations cutting through or bowing around precipitates. Instead, it emerges from collective, multi-dislocation interactions involving accumulation at interfaces, storage within precipitates, and precipitate-mediated multiplication.
AI.motivation: The classical cutting-versus-bowing dichotomy for precipitation strengthening is incomplete because in situ experiments cannot resolve the coupled real-time evolution of dislocation networks and nanoprecipitates at atomic scales.
AI.method: Large-scale atomistic simulations that fully capture the coupled, real-time dynamics of dislocation networks and nanoprecipitates.
AI.result: Strengthening arises as an emergent collective phenomenon driven by concurrent, multi-dislocation interactions, including dislocation accumulation at interfaces, storage within precipitates, and precipitate-mediated multiplication in the matrix.
AI.conclusion: The findings establish a mechanistic framework that transcends traditional cutting/bowing models and provides a new foundation for predicting strengthening behavior.

title: Creation and motion of antiferromagnetic skyrmions by edge manipulation
summary: Magnetic racetrack architectures that use topological magnetic particles to store information are one of the most promising concepts for future storage applications. Antiferromagnetic racetracks are particularly appealing as they are not susceptible to external magnetic fields. State-of-the-art racetracks use magnetic fields, spin-transfer and spin-orbit torques caused by electric currents to move the bits across the entire circuit. However, the application of currents in many antiferromagnetic racetracks is limited because many of them are insulating. Recently, however, a concept for ferromagnetic racetrack memories that are free of global driving forces has been proposed. It has been demonstrated that various topological entities can be generated and transported over long distances solely through local magnetization rotation at the sample boundaries, independent of global driving forces. Here, we demonstrate that the local rotation of magnetization at the boundary of an antiferromagnetic sample can be exploited in racetracks to efficiently generate and transmit antiferromagnetic skyrmions. Additionally, we demonstrate that local switching of staggered magnetization at the edge of an antiferromagnetic racetrack can be even more successful than the rotational procedure. A comparison of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic processing of skyrmionic bits, together with energy considerations, shows that this procedure is fairly efficient in antiferromagnets.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that local magnetization rotation at the boundaries of antiferromagnetic samples can efficiently generate and transmit antiferromagnetic skyrmions in racetracks, offering a driving-force-free alternative to current-driven methods, and shows that local edge switching is even more effective than rotational procedures, with favorable energy efficiency compared to ferromagnetic counterparts.
AI.motivation: Antiferromagnetic racetracks are appealing for storage due to immunity to external magnetic fields, but many are insulating, limiting the use of electric-current-driven mechanisms (spin-transfer and spin-orbit torques). A driving-force-free approach is needed for antiferromagnetic racetrack memories.
AI.method: The authors propose using local rotation of magnetization at the boundary of an antiferromagnetic sample to generate and transport antiferromagnetic skyrmions, and compare it with local switching of staggered magnetization at the edge. They compare the performance with ferromagnetic skyrmion processing and analyze energy considerations.
AI.result: Local boundary rotation efficiently generates and transmits antiferromagnetic skyrmions. Local edge switching of staggered magnetization outperforms the rotational procedure. The antiferromagnetic processing is fairly energy-efficient compared to ferromagnetic counterparts.
AI.conclusion: Local magnetization manipulation at sample boundaries is a viable, efficient, and driving-force-free mechanism for antiferromagnetic racetrack memories, with edge switching being the superior strategy.

title: Effect of the hyperbolic photon mode on the metal insulator transition in a proximate material
summary: The hyperbolic mode (HM) refers to a polariton mode where the dielectric function is negative in some direction of propagation. Within a frequency window the light occupies a greatly expanded region in momentum space. We compute the photon density of states and find that the zero point fluctuation in the RMS electric field can reach $MV/cm$, comparable to the largest field used in pump probe experiments in the THz scale. The HM in hexagonal Boron Nitride (hBN) has been under intense study and we consider placing a material that is near the Mott transition directly on top hBN. We find that a substantial shift in the metal-insulator transition is possible, but the effect decays rapidly with distance, so that only a few monolayers are affected. We provide estimates and suggestions for a number of materials of interest.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates hyperbolic modes in polariton systems, showing they produce intense zero-point electric fields (MV/cm) in the THz range, and demonstrates that placing a Mott-transition material on hBN can shift the metal-insulator transition, though the effect is limited to a few monolayers.
AI.motivation: To explore the impact of hyperbolic modes (HMs) on nearby materials, specifically whether the large zero-point fluctuations in the electric field can influence the metal-insulator transition in materials near the Mott transition.
AI.method: Computes the photon density of states to quantify zero-point RMS electric field fluctuations in hyperbolic modes, and models the effect of placing a Mott-transition material directly on hexagonal Boron Nitride (hBN) to assess shifts in the metal-insulator transition as a function of distance.
AI.result: Zero-point fluctuations in the RMS electric field can reach MV/cm, comparable to strong pump-probe fields in the THz range. A substantial shift in the metal-insulator transition is possible when a Mott material is placed on hBN, but the effect decays rapidly with distance, affecting only a few monolayers.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic modes can produce extremely large vacuum fields that may locally tune the metal-insulator transition, but the spatial range is limited to a few monolayers; suggestions for suitable materials are provided.

title: Accelerating Kinetic Fokker-Planck Simulations via a GPU-Native Deep Neural Network Surrogate: Application to Rarefied Internal and Hypersonic External Flows
summary: Particle-based Fokker--Planck (FP) models provide an efficient kinetic alternative to direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) in slip and early transitional gas flow regimes, but advanced cubic-FP closures require repeated cell-wise moment evaluation and small dense linear solves. This work develops and validates a GPU-native neural surrogate that replaces the deterministic cubic-FP closure calculation inside the particle simulation loop. The trained weights are evaluated directly with batched \texttt{CuPy} operations, avoiding CPU--GPU transfers during online deployment. The validation emphasizes quantitative evidence: component-level runtime profiles, break-even cost analysis including offline costs, conservation and stability diagnostics, particle-per-cell sensitivity, a direct time-averaged coefficient audit, and covariance-based entropy-proxy fidelity checks. The Couette case is retained as a compact, dimensionless verification problem, while the main internal-flow validation is a 2D lid-driven cavity tested by complete simulation conditions, including unseen moderately rarefied cases at nominal $Kn=0.5$ and $Kn=1.0$. For the hypersonic cylinder, a particle-moment covariance-based entropy-fidelity audit is performed on the front stagnation line and in the cell-centered near-wall gas layer. The same deployed neural $C/Γ$ closure used for the cylinder flow fields closely reproduces the equilibrium and Gaussian kinetic entropy profiles over the reported front-line and near-wall gas bins; these profiles are used as a relatively exact-FP/ML-FP audit. The study establishes GPU-native learned closure as a practical route to accelerating cubic-FP rarefied-flow solvers, delivering substantial online speedups while retaining the macroscopic, high-order, and entropy-proxy structure of the reference kinetic model.

AI.tldr: This paper develops and validates a GPU-native neural surrogate that replaces the deterministic cubic-FP closure calculation inside particle simulations, demonstrating substantial online speedups for rarefied gas flows while preserving macroscopic, high-order, and entropy-proxy fidelity.
AI.motivation: Particle-based Fokker-Planck models are efficient kinetic alternatives to DSMC in slip/transitional regimes, but advanced cubic-FP closures require expensive cell-wise moment evaluation and small dense linear solves, motivating a faster surrogate.
AI.method: A GPU-native neural surrogate is trained offline to replace the cubic-FP closure calculation; trained weights are evaluated via batched CuPy operations to avoid CPU-GPU transfers during online deployment in the particle simulation loop.
AI.result: Substantial online speedups with quantitative evidence: component-level runtime profiles, break-even cost analysis, conservation/stability diagnostics, particle-per-cell sensitivity, time-averaged coefficient audit, and covariance-based entropy-proxy fidelity checks on Couette flow, 2D lid-driven cavity (Kn=0.5, 1.0), and hypersonic cylinder cases.
AI.conclusion: GPU-native learned closure is a practical route to accelerating cubic-FP rarefied-flow solvers, delivering substantial speedups while retaining macroscopic, high-order, and entropy-proxy structure of the reference kinetic model.

title: Staggered Virtual-Loop-Current Order in Pseudospin-1 Dirac Flat Bands
summary: Although interactions are known to generate exotic phases in pseudospin-1/2 flat-band Dirac materials, it remains an open question whether the higher-pseudospin systems could realize entirely new types of orders and, if so, how such orders are governed by the nature of the underlying Dirac states. Here, we demonstrate that short-range interactions can drive a staggered virtual-loop-current (SVLC) order together with a $\sqrt{3}\times\sqrt{3}$ charge order in a partially filled pseudospin-1 Dirac flat band of the dice lattice. The virtual loop currents are shown to originate from interaction-driven quantum fluctuations of charge densities and exhibit alternating circulation between the neighboring triangular plaquettes. The resulting spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking is found to induce finite intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity and orbital magnetization. The SVLC state is shown to be the lowest energy solution in restricted real-space Hartree-Fock calculations in the weakly interacting regime. The pseudospin-1 Dirac cones enter the SVLC order through the equivalence of their flat-band wavefunctions, and unlike the pseudospin-1/2 Dirac systems, do not rely on the presence of well-defined low-energy valleys in the electronic spectrum. Our study establishes higher-pseudospin Dirac systems as a new platform for investigating exotic emergent orders in flat-band physics.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that short-range interactions in a pseudospin-1 Dirac flat band (dice lattice) can drive a staggered virtual-loop-current (SVLC) order with √3×√3 charge order, breaking time-reversal symmetry and inducing anomalous Hall conductivity and orbital magnetization, establishing higher-pseudospin Dirac systems as a new platform for exotic flat-band orders.
AI.motivation: To determine whether higher-pseudospin (beyond pseudospin-1/2) flat-band Dirac systems can realize entirely new types of orders, and how such orders are governed by the nature of the underlying Dirac states.
AI.method: Restricted real-space Hartree-Fock calculations in the weakly interacting regime, analyzing short-range interactions in a partially filled pseudospin-1 Dirac flat band of the dice lattice.
AI.result: Short-range interactions drive a staggered virtual-loop-current (SVLC) order with √3×√3 charge order; the SVLC state is the lowest energy solution in the weakly interacting regime. Spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking yields finite intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity and orbital magnetization. Pseudospin-1 Dirac cones enter the SVLC order through equivalence of their flat-band wavefunctions, not requiring well-defined low-energy valleys.
AI.conclusion: Higher-pseudospin Dirac systems constitute a new platform for investigating exotic emergent orders in flat-band physics.

title: Universality in the target arrival statistics of non-conservative search processes
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures (6 pages of Supp. Mat.)
summary: Stochastic search processes in which searchers are continuously introduced to and removed from a target search domain are fundamental to a wide class of physical and artificial systems. The theory of such non-conservative search processes is, however, much less developed than for search processes with a fixed number of particles. Here we exploit a natural mapping between non-conservative stochastic search and queueing theory to derive the full time-dependent distribution of target arrivals under minimal assumptions on the underlying search process. Remarkably, we find that the steady-state inter-arrival time distribution is exactly exponential, regardless of the details of the search process, showing a robust universality that emerges directly from the queueing framework. Thus, counterintuitively, the arrival statistics of a non-conservative search process are much simpler than sequential search-and-capture processes involving a fixed number of searchers. This has major implications for target resource accumulation, where the delivery of resources is counter-balanced by their downstream consumption.

AI.tldr: This paper derives the full time-dependent distribution of target arrivals for non-conservative stochastic search processes (where searchers are continuously added and removed) by mapping them to queueing theory. It finds that the steady-state inter-arrival time distribution is universally exponential regardless of search process details, and discusses implications for target resource accumulation.
AI.motivation: Non-conservative search processes (with continuous introduction and removal of searchers) are fundamental to many physical and artificial systems, but their theory is much less developed than that of conservative search processes with a fixed number of particles.
AI.method: The authors exploit a natural mapping between non-conservative stochastic search and queueing theory to derive the full time-dependent distribution of target arrivals under minimal assumptions on the underlying search process.
AI.result: The steady-state inter-arrival time distribution is exactly exponential regardless of the details of the search process, demonstrating a robust universality emerging from the queueing framework.
AI.conclusion: Non-conservative search processes yield simpler arrival statistics than sequential search-and-capture with a fixed number of searchers, with major implications for target resource accumulation where resource delivery is counter-balanced by downstream consumption.

title: Stitching Molecular Worlds Together with Physics-Coupled Diffusion Models
summary: Complex chemical systems often contain multiple components or large molecules, giving rise to substantial chemical and conformational complexity. Modeling the structures of these systems is crucial for mechanistic understanding of chemical processes and rational design, but remains highly challenging for both conventional theoretical approaches and machine learning. Here, we introduce physical-interaction-coupled diffusion models (PICDiff), a framework that couples independently trained diffusion models for subsystems of a complex system through explicit bonded and nonbonded interactions during inference. PICDiff reduces the difficulty of applying generative models to chemically and conformationally complex systems by decomposing them into smaller subsystems that are less complex and more amenable to machine-learning-based modeling. Using peptide-polymer binding and polymer conformation sampling as examples, we demonstrate that PICDiff can quantitatively sample conformations and model the thermodynamics of complex chemical systems. These results show that PICDiff provides a general and practical approach for modeling complex chemical systems by combining learned models of simpler molecular subsystems through physical interactions.

AI.tldr: PICDiff couples independently trained diffusion models for subsystems of a complex chemical system through explicit physical interactions, enabling conformation sampling and thermodynamic modeling of complex systems like peptide-polymer binding and polymer conformation.
AI.motivation: Modeling structures of complex chemical systems (multiple components, large molecules) is crucial for mechanistic understanding and rational design but remains challenging for both conventional theoretical and machine learning approaches.
AI.method: PICDiff decomposes complex systems into smaller, less complex subsystems, trains independent diffusion models for each subsystem, and couples them through explicit bonded and nonbonded physical interactions during inference.
AI.result: Quantitative conformation sampling and thermodynamic modeling were achieved for peptide-polymer binding and polymer conformation sampling.
AI.conclusion: PICDiff provides a general and practical approach for modeling complex chemical systems by combining learned models of simpler molecular subsystems through physical interactions.

title: Fermi-Level-Dependent Defect Chemistry and Oxygen Evolution Reaction Activity of Fe-Doped and Oxygen-Deficient \ce{SrTiO3}(001)
summary: The oxygen evolution reaction (OER) on perovskite oxides is controlled by the interplay of dopant chemistry, defect charge states, and surface segregation, yet these factors are rarely treated on equal footing. Using first-principles density functional theory, we investigate how Fe dopants (\FeTi{}) and oxygen vacancies (\VO{}) in different charge states affect the OER on TiO$_2$-terminated \ce{SrTiO3}(001). We combine charge-dependent defect formation energies, segregation energies, and charge transition levels with OER free-energy profiles obtained in the computational hydrogen electrode framework. Neutral \FeTix{} preserves near-pristine activity, with overpotentials of $0.43$--$0.48$~V compared to $0.45$~V for the pristine surface, whereas the reduced states \FeTip{} and \FeTipp{} raise the overpotential to as much as $1.35$~V when intermediates bind to Ti sites adjacent to surface Fe. Oxygen vacancies segregate to the surface across the entire band gap ($ΔE_\mathrm{seg} = -0.50$ to $-0.80$~eV) but do not improve the activity: \VOx{} and \VOp{} overstabilize oxygenated intermediates ($η$ up to $2.13$~V), and only \VOpp{} retains a balanced pathway ($η= 0.45$~V in the bulk-like region). Because the stable charge state and the segregation tendency of each defect are set by the Fermi level, the OER overpotential itself becomes a Fermi-level-dependent quantity. These results establish Fermi-level engineering as a framework for assessing and tuning defect-mediated OER activity in perovskite oxides.

AI.tldr: This paper uses DFT to study how Fe dopants and oxygen vacancies in different charge states affect the OER on SrTiO3(001), showing that neutral Fe preserves near-pristine activity while reduced Fe states and oxygen vacancies degrade performance, and establishing that OER overpotential is Fermi-level-dependent.
AI.motivation: Dopant chemistry, defect charge states, and surface segregation control OER on perovskite oxides but are rarely treated together. The authors aim to investigate these factors on equal footing using SrTiO3 as a model system.
AI.method: First-principles DFT combined with charge-dependent defect formation energies, segregation energies, charge transition levels, and computational hydrogen electrode framework for OER free-energy profiles.
AI.result: Neutral FeTi preserves near-pristine activity (η=0.43-0.48V vs 0.45V pristine); reduced Fe states raise η up to 1.35V. Oxygen vacancies segregate to surface (ΔEseg=-0.50 to -0.80eV) but don't improve activity: VOx and VOp overstabilize intermediates (η up to 2.13V), only VOpp retains balance (η=0.45V).
AI.conclusion: OER overpotential is a Fermi-level-dependent quantity due to charge state and segregation dependence on Fermi level; Fermi-level engineering is established as a framework for tuning defect-mediated OER activity in perovskite oxides.

title: Interaction and non-Hermiticity controlled transmission in extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger models
summary: We study the transport characteristics of an extended version of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model with next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) interactions and non-Hermitian onsite energies. We observed that transport in such a system is significantly modified by the NNN interaction and the non-Hermitian terms. The transmission coefficient exhibits oscillatory behavior as the strength of the NNN interaction varies in a fixed-length chain. Moreover, the transmission coefficient also shows oscillation with system size for a fixed strength of the NNN interaction. We find that novel oscillatory behavior of the transmission coefficient, arising form the NNN interaction, is a unique feature of such a model and has not been reported previously. The presence of the non-Hermitian terms also enhances/reduces the transmission coefficient depending on the values of the other system parameters like intra-, inter- and NNN hopping. It appears from our study that both the NNN interaction and the non-Hermiticity introduce significant changes in the transport properties of the extended SSH chain, which are not observed in the standard Hermitian nearest-neighbour variant of the SSH model.

AI.tldr: This paper studies transport in an extended SSH model with next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) interactions and non-Hermitian onsite energies, finding novel oscillatory transmission behavior and significant modifications due to NNN and non-Hermitian terms.
AI.motivation: To understand how next-nearest-neighbor interactions and non-Hermitian onsite terms modify transport properties beyond the standard Hermitian nearest-neighbor SSH model, and to reveal new oscillatory transmission features not previously reported.
AI.method: The authors analyze transport in an extended Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) model incorporating next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) interactions and non-Hermitian onsite energies, studying transmission coefficient dependence on NNN strength, system size, and hopping parameters.
