AI.result: Near-perfect lattice matching (~3.5 Å, matching equilibrium HCP spacing of cryogenic D₂) yields coherent layer-by-layer epitaxial growth with HCP-dominated near-single crystals, minimal dislocations, and ultra-smooth inner surfaces. Large mismatch causes island-like growth, polycrystalline mixed HCP/FCC phases, elevated defects, and increased surface roughness. Interfacial stress localizes within 2-3 molecular layers near the interface.
AI.conclusion: Substrate lattice matching is established as a key principle for ablator inner-surface engineering in ICF cryogenic targets, offering atomic-scale guidance for growing high-quality single-crystal DT fuel layers with optimal smoothness.

title: Multiband transport hierarchy and large Nernst effect in EuAuBi: Establishing a Nernst scaling for asymmetric multiband systems
summary: In correlated materials, coexisting pockets of vastly different carrier densities raise two fundamental questions: which pocket governs the various transport coefficients, and does the conventional Nernst scaling $ν/T \propto μ/E_F$, originally derived for single-band systems, still hold? We address both questions in the polar semimetal EuAuBi, where a dilute electron pocket ($n_e \sim 10^{16}~\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$) coexists with a dense hole pocket ($n_h \sim 10^{21}~\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$). We find a clear hierarchy: the hole pocket dominates the longitudinal resistivity; the Hall effect crosses from electron- to hole-dominance with increasing field; the Seebeck coefficient is dominated by the electron pocket at low temperature and by both pockets at high temperature. Remarkably, the Nernst effect is governed entirely by the ultrahigh-mobility electron pocket, yielding a large low-field signal of $\sim 5~μ\mathrm{V/K}$ near 1~T at 202~K, comparable to anomalous Nernst signals in magnetic Weyl semimetals. By analyzing the two-band thermoelectric conductivity, we show that the Nernst coefficient follows a scaling $ν/T \propto μ_e/{E_{F, tot}}$. This scaling originates from a compensation between the electron-to-hole conductivity ratio and the Fermi-energy ratio, establishing that the large Nernst effect is a semiclassical multiband phenomenon rather than a topological Berry-curvature contribution. This understanding advances the thermoelectric transport physics of multiband electronic systems and offers a guiding principle for low-field transverse thermoelectric design.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates transport in the polar semimetal EuAuBi, where a dilute high-mobility electron pocket coexists with a dense hole pocket. It reveals a hierarchy of transport coefficients: hole pocket dominates resistivity, electron pocket dominates the Nernst effect. The Nernst scaling $ν/T \propto \mu_e/E_{F,tot}$ is derived from multiband compensation, showing the large Nernst signal is semiclassical, not topological.
AI.motivation: To understand which carrier pocket governs different transport coefficients in multiband correlated materials, and to test whether the conventional single-band Nernst scaling law $ν/T \propto \mu/E_F$ still holds when vastly different carrier densities coexist.
AI.method: Experimental transport measurements (resistivity, Hall, Seebeck, Nernst) on the polar semimetal EuAuBi, combined with two-band thermoelectric conductivity analysis to derive the scaling relation.
AI.result: The Nernst effect is dominated entirely by the ultrahigh-mobility electron pocket, yielding a large low-field signal ~5 μV/K near 1 T at 202 K. The Nernst coefficient follows a modified scaling $ν/T \propto \mu_e/E_{F,tot}$, arising from compensation between the electron-to-hole conductivity ratio and the Fermi-energy ratio.
AI.conclusion: The large Nernst effect in EuAuBi is a semiclassical multiband phenomenon rather than a topological Berry-curvature contribution. This advances thermoelectric transport physics of multiband systems and provides a guiding principle for low-field transverse thermoelectric design.

title: Persistence Properties of a Phase-ordering System with Competing Dynamics
summary: We investigate the persistence properties during phase ordering in the two-dimensional ($d=2$) Ising model evolving under competing nonconserved spin-flip and conserved spin-exchange dynamics by means of Monte Carlo simulations at zero temperature. We examine three distinct persistence probabilities: (i) the total persistence probability, defined as the probability that a lattice site has never experienced a change in the sign of the spin residing there; (ii) the spin-flip persistence probability, which exclusively measures the fraction of sites that have never undergone a spin-flip event; and (iii) the composite persistence probability, defined as the fraction of sites that have experienced neither a spin-flip nor a spin-exchange event. In the asymptotic regime, both the total and spin-flip persistence probabilities exhibit identical power-law decay, irrespective of the relative occurrence probability of the spin-flip move $p_r$. The corresponding persistence exponent $θ_i \approx 0.225$, is found to be consistent with the value reported for systems evolving purely under nonconserved dynamics. We further demonstrate that both persistence measures satisfy the scaling relation $d-d_f^i=θ_i/α_i$, where $d_f^i$ is the fractal dimension of the corresponding persistence lattice and $α_i\approx 1/2$ characterizes the asymptotic power-law growth of spatially correlated regions of non-persistent spins. In contrast, although the composite persistence probability also exhibits asymptotic power-law decay, both the corresponding persistence exponent $θ_{\rm c}$ and the fractal dimension $d_f^{\rm c}$ of the persistence lattice show strong dependence on $p_r$. Combined with the presence of a universal growth exponent $α_{\rm c}\approx 1/2$, this leads to the breakdown of the scaling relation among the characteristic exponents for the composite persistence.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates persistence probabilities during phase ordering in the 2D Ising model under competing nonconserved (spin-flip) and conserved (spin-exchange) dynamics via zero-temperature Monte Carlo simulations. Total and spin-flip persistence probabilities show identical power-law decay with exponent θ_i ≈ 0.225, independent of spin-flip probability p_r, satisfying a scaling relation. Composite persistence shows p_r-dependent exponents and breaks the scaling relation.
AI.motivation: To understand persistence properties in phase-ordering kinetics under competing nonconserved and conserved dynamics, and to test scaling relations among persistence exponents.
AI.method: Monte Carlo simulations at zero temperature of the 2D Ising model evolving under competing spin-flip (nonconserved) and spin-exchange (conserved) dynamics, measuring three distinct persistence probabilities.
AI.result: Total and spin-flip persistence decay with exponent θ_i ≈ 0.225, independent of p_r, matching purely nonconserved dynamics. Composite persistence exponent θ_c and fractal dimension d_f^c depend strongly on p_r, while growth exponent α_c ≈ 1/2 is universal. The scaling relation holds for total/spin-flip but breaks for composite persistence.
AI.conclusion: Total and spin-flip persistence are robust to the introduction of conserved dynamics, while composite persistence is sensitive to the competition between dynamics and violates the scaling relation.

title: Nonlocal Orbital-Free Kinetic Energy Functional from the Jellium-with-Gap Model for Finite Systems
comment: Accepted in J. Chem. Theory Comput. (2026)
summary: The quasi-linear scaling of orbital-free density functional theory (OF-DFT) with system size makes it a computationally efficient alternative to conventional Kohn--Sham density functional theory for many condensed-matter applications. However, its applicability remains limited, particularly for finite systems such as molecular clusters, due to the lack of accurate kinetic energy density functionals. In this context, the development of nonlocal kinetic energy density functionals (NL-KEDFs) has significantly advanced the practical utility of OF-DFT. Here, following an alternative formulation based on the linear-response kernel derived from the jellium-with-gap model (JGM), we develop an NL-KEDF capable of accurately describing the diverse density regimes characteristic of finite systems, including molecular clusters. Benchmark calculations, together with an analysis of the corresponding Pauli potentials, demonstrate that the proposed functional achieves higher accuracy than state-of-the-art orbital-free approaches for finite systems. Furthermore, the optical properties computed using the present method show good agreement with reference results, highlighting its reliability. These results indicate that the proposed NL-KEDF provides a robust and efficient framework for extending OF-DFT to finite systems, with potential implications for nanomaterial design and a deeper understanding of nanoscale phenomena.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a nonlocal kinetic energy density functional (NL-KEDF) based on the jellium-with-gap model (JGM) for orbital-free density functional theory (OF-DFT), enabling accurate description of finite systems like molecular clusters, with benchmark results showing higher accuracy than existing orbital-free approaches and reliable optical properties.
AI.motivation: OF-DFT is efficient due to quasi-linear scaling but lacks accurate kinetic energy density functionals for finite systems (e.g., molecular clusters), limiting its applicability. The development of NL-KEDFs has advanced OF-DFT, but further improvement is needed for finite systems.
AI.method: The authors propose an alternative NL-KEDF formulation based on the linear-response kernel derived from the jellium-with-gap model (JGM), designed to accurately describe diverse density regimes in finite systems.
AI.result: Benchmark calculations and Pauli potential analysis show the proposed functional achieves higher accuracy than state-of-the-art orbital-free approaches for finite systems. Computed optical properties agree well with reference results.
AI.conclusion: The proposed NL-KEDF offers a robust and efficient framework for extending OF-DFT to finite systems, with potential implications for nanomaterial design and understanding nanoscale phenomena.

title: Spin-dependent electron transfer through a ring-wire coupled junction: Role of in-plane electric field
summary: We study spin-dependent transport in a hybrid magnetic system, where a non-magnetic (NM) wire is coupled to a side-attached antiferromagnetic (AFM) mesoscopic ring, placed between two non-magnetic electrodes subject to an in-plane electric field oriented perpendicular to the NM wire. The system is described within a tight-binding (TB) framework, and transport properties are computed using the non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism. We consider two junction configurations distinguished by the wire-ring coupling: a single-coupled junction and a double-coupled junction. In the single-coupled configuration, the coupling geometry alone breaks the spin symmetry, yielding a finite spin polarization (SP) even without any external field. The in-plane electric field further enhances the symmetry breaking in both configurations, serving as an efficient tuning parameter that drives the SP nearly $100\%$ in the low-bias region. In the double-coupled configuration, spin symmetry is preserved in the absence of the external field, and the electric field acts as a sole source of symmetry breaking, producing a large SP. Finite temperature effects and different system sizes are examined, confirming the robustness of the observed features. To validate the findings over a wide parameter space, we considered different sets of parameters and found that the key signatures remain unchanged. Our results demonstrate that such hybrid structures are promising candidates for realizing an externally controllable spintronic device in low-dimensional systems.

AI.tldr: A hybrid NM wire coupled to an AFM ring, driven by an in-plane electric field, achieves nearly 100% spin polarization at low bias, controllable via coupling geometry and external field.
AI.motivation: To explore externally controllable spintronic devices in low-dimensional systems by studying spin-dependent transport in a hybrid NM/AFM structure.
AI.method: Tight-binding (TB) model with non-equilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism; single-coupled and double-coupled junction configurations; in-plane electric field applied perpendicular to the NM wire.
AI.result: Single-coupled junction breaks spin symmetry via coupling geometry alone; in-plane electric field enhances symmetry breaking, achieving nearly 100% SP at low bias. Double-coupled junction requires electric field for symmetry breaking, also producing large SP. Results robust against temperature and system size variations.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid NM/AFM structures with side-attached rings are promising candidates for controllable spintronic devices in low-dimensional systems.

title: Superconducting diode effect via Floquet topological Fulde-Ferrell phase in driven Rashba nanowire
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures (main text) + 3 pages, 2 figures (supplementary materials). Comments are welcome
summary: Much has been studied on Floquet engineering in Rashba nanowire model regarding topological superconductivity hosting Majorana $0$- and anomalous $π$-modes, here we theoretically investigate the possible emergence of finite momentum Fulde-Ferrell (FF) superconducting state in quasi-energy of the above model under the periodic modulation of in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic fields while the static limit does not host a FF ground state. We demonstrate controllable switching between Floquet Majorana $0$- and $π$-modes via reversal of the supercurrent direction, revealing pronounced nonreciprocal supercurrent signatures which is a manifestation of the FF pairing. We validate the onset of FF pairing following a self-consistent mean-field analysis where externally applied supercurrent facilitates nonreciprocal signatures in quasi-energy spectra. The above findings directly indicates to the intriguing phenomenon of superconducting diode effect (SDE). The drive amplitude serves as a parameter to regulate the diode efficiency with chemical potential. Our study thus reveals a rich interplay between Floquet topological superconductivity and finite-momentum FF pairing, providing a tunable way to switch between different Floquet Majorana modes and realize the SDE with high efficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically investigates the emergence of finite-momentum Fulde-Ferrell (FF) superconducting states in a Floquet-engineered Rashba nanowire model under periodic magnetic field modulation, demonstrating controllable switching between Floquet Majorana 0- and π-modes via supercurrent reversal and realizing a high-efficiency superconducting diode effect (SDE).
AI.motivation: To explore whether finite-momentum FF pairing can emerge in the quasi-energy spectrum of a Rashba nanowire under periodic driving (where static limit does not host FF), and to understand the interplay between Floquet topological superconductivity and nonreciprocal supercurrent phenomena.
AI.method: Floquet engineering with periodic in-plane and out-of-plane magnetic field modulation; self-consistent mean-field analysis; externally applied supercurrent to probe nonreciprocal quasi-energy spectra.
AI.result: Controllable switching between Floquet Majorana 0- and π-modes via supercurrent direction reversal; pronounced nonreciprocal supercurrent signatures as manifestation of FF pairing; drive amplitude regulates diode efficiency with chemical potential.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals a rich interplay between Floquet topological superconductivity and finite-momentum FF pairing, offering a tunable platform to switch between different Floquet Majorana modes and realize high-efficiency superconducting diode effect.

title: Quantum oscillations in proximity to high-angular-momentum band inversion
summary: Quantum oscillations provide a fundamental probe of electronic structure in magnetic fields, revealing the Fermi surface topology in metals, and/or the quasiparticle properties even in the insulating regimes. Here we study quantum oscillations in minimal models of high-angular-momentum (HAM) band inversion for both a chiral two-band model and a time-reversal-invariant four-band model. In the former case, finite oscillations can appear at the hybridized Chern-insulating regime due to thermal-activated excitations. In the latter case, interference between the two time-reversal-related blocks drives a strong deviation from the Lifshitz-Kosevich form, producing a non-monotonic temperature dependence of the oscillation amplitude and characteristic suppression temperatures whose number follows the angular momentum $l$. These results identify experimentally accessible signatures of HAM band inversion and provide a framework for other discrete-symmetry-related hybridizations and excitonic pairings.

AI.tldr: This paper studies quantum oscillations in high-angular-momentum (HAM) band inversion models, finding that chiral two-band models show finite oscillations in Chern-insulating regimes via thermal activation, while time-reversal-invariant four-band models exhibit non-monotonic temperature dependence of oscillation amplitudes with characteristic suppression temperatures scaling with angular momentum $l$, deviating from the standard Lifshitz-Kosevich form.
AI.motivation: To understand quantum oscillation phenomena in high-angular-momentum band inversion systems and identify experimentally accessible signatures that distinguish them from conventional band structures.
AI.method: Study quantum oscillations in minimal models of HAM band inversion: a chiral two-band model and a time-reversal-invariant four-band model, analyzing their temperature dependence and oscillation amplitude behavior.
AI.result: In the chiral two-band model, finite oscillations emerge in the hybridized Chern-insulating regime via thermal-activated excitations. In the four-band model, interference between time-reversal-related blocks produces non-monotonic temperature dependence of oscillation amplitude with characteristic suppression temperatures scaling with $l$.
AI.conclusion: The identified signatures provide experimentally accessible probes of HAM band inversion and a framework for understanding other discrete-symmetry-related hybridizations and excitonic pairings.

title: Geometric decomposition of the $d$-dimensional hard-sphere partition function
summary: We introduce a geometric decomposition of the hard-sphere partition function. Using a close-packing-inspired geometric bound on the available insertion volume, made rigorous when a corresponding local density certificate is available, we establish a reference upper bound $Q^\ast$ on the configurational integral. Factoring this upper bound out of the statistical geometric partition function of Speedy yields a new form for the $d$-dimensional partition function, $Q(N,V,T)=Q^\ast \exp(-N \mathcal{J})$, where $\mathcal{J}$ depends strictly on the boundary-to-volume ratio of the voids and the close-packing density. Overall, this work deepens our statistical geometric understanding of the hard-sphere system.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a geometric decomposition of the hard-sphere partition function using a close-packing-inspired bound on available insertion volume, establishing a reference upper bound Q* and a new form Q = Q* exp(-N J) where J depends on boundary-to-volume ratio of voids and close-packing density.
AI.motivation: To deepen the statistical geometric understanding of the hard-sphere system by providing a rigorous geometric bound on the configurational integral.
AI.method: A geometric decomposition of the hard-sphere partition function using a close-packing-inspired bound on available insertion volume, made rigorous via a local density certificate.
AI.result: Established a reference upper bound Q* on the configurational integral; derived a new form for the d-dimensional partition function: Q(N,V,T) = Q* exp(-N J).
AI.conclusion: The work deepens the statistical geometric understanding of the hard-sphere system by showing J depends strictly on the boundary-to-volume ratio of voids and close-packing density.

title: A Unified Dielectric-Dependent Hybrid Functional for Accurate Band Gaps across Dimensions
summary: Predicting fundamental band gaps across material classes and dimensionalities remains a central challenge in electronic-structure theory. Here, we show that intrinsic dielectric screening provides a unified control parameter for nonlocal exchange from bulk to low-dimensional and heterogeneous materials. We introduce a geometry-independent dielectric response and incorporate it self-consistently into a nonempirical screened-dielectric-dependent hybrid functional. Benchmarks for 100 materials spanning bulk, two-dimensional, one-dimensional, and mixed-dimensional systems show near-GW accuracy at the computational cost of generalized Kohn-Sham theory. These results reveal a screening-exchange-gap relation in which reduced dimensionality weakens intrinsic dielectric screening, strengthens nonlocal exchange, and drives the opening of fundamental gaps.

AI.tldr: A new hybrid functional using a geometry-independent dielectric response achieves near-GW accuracy for band gaps across bulk, 2D, 1D, and mixed-dimensional materials by unifying nonlocal exchange through intrinsic dielectric screening.
AI.motivation: Predicting fundamental band gaps across different material classes and dimensionalities is a central challenge; existing methods lack a unified framework.
AI.method: Introduced a geometry-independent dielectric response, incorporated self-consistently into a nonempirical screened-dielectric-dependent hybrid functional.
AI.result: Benchmarks for 100 materials (bulk, 2D, 1D, mixed-dimensional) show near-GW accuracy at generalized Kohn-Sham computational cost.
AI.conclusion: A screening-exchange-gap relation exists where reduced dimensionality weakens dielectric screening, strengthens nonlocal exchange, and opens fundamental gaps.

title: Intervalley coherence and flavor polarization in three-valley moiré systems
summary: We investigate interaction-induced symmetry breaking in moiré superlattices created by twisting two identical materials where the electronic low-energy degrees of freedom reside in the vicinity of the $M$ points. Based on general symmetry arguments, we identify and classify the possible candidate instabilities that, besides flavor polarized states, also involve a variety of intervalley-coherent (IVC) orders. This complexity is related primarily to the presence of three valleys, instead of the well-studied scenario of two, e.g., in graphene: IVC states can couple all three valleys identically, with a non-trivial sign structure, or even with different magnitudes. We study the energetics using an analytical strong-coupling framework and unrestricted Hartree-Fock applied to the full continuum model, with very good agreement between the two approaches. Interestingly, depending on stacking, IVC instabilities not only appear due to superexchange at moderate bandwidths, but also deep in the strong-coupling regime as a result of deviations from the flat-metric condition. Our work demonstrates that twisted $M$-point materials provide a rich playground for complex correlated physics and highlights differences and similarities to twisted multilayer graphene.

AI.tldr: Investigates interaction-driven symmetry breaking in twisted moiré superlattices where low-energy electrons reside near M points, identifying various intervalley-coherent (IVC) orders beyond flavor-polarized states due to the presence of three valleys. Using analytical strong-coupling and Hartree-Fock methods, the study shows IVC instabilities arise from superexchange at moderate bandwidths and from flat-metric deviations in strong coupling, highlighting rich correlated physics distinct from twisted graphene.
AI.motivation: To understand interaction-induced symmetry breaking in moiré superlattices with three-valley electronic structures (M-point materials), which are less explored than the two-valley case (e.g., graphene), and to classify possible exotic ordered phases beyond flavor polarization.
AI.method: General symmetry arguments for classifying instabilities, analytical strong-coupling framework, and unrestricted Hartree-Fock calculations on the full continuum model.
AI.result: Identified various IVC orders coupling all three valleys identically, with non-trivial sign structure, or with different magnitudes. IVC instabilities arise both from superexchange at moderate bandwidths and from deviations from flat-metric condition in strong coupling. Good agreement between analytical and numerical approaches.
AI.conclusion: Twisted M-point materials offer a rich platform for complex correlated physics, with both similarities and differences compared to twisted multilayer graphene systems.

title: Refining Unified Colored-Noise Approximation
summary: Countless biological and physical systems experience fluctuations that exhibit non-trivial temporal correlations. The Unified Colored-Noise Approximation (UCNA) is a framework providing an approximate description of such stochastic dynamics with colored noise, valid in the limits of vanishing and infinite correlation time of the noise. We first pinpoint and address some criticalities in its original derivation, recasting the result through a time-scale separation procedure. By using our approach, we derive the next-to-leading order correction to the dynamics in both limiting regimes, and highlight the relevant physical scalings of these approximations. Our result helps frame the limits of validity of both the original and the refined formulas, especially in comparison with those derived through different approximation procedures. We show our findings in two paradigmatic examples, a quartic potential and a stochastic logistic growth with multiplicative noise.

AI.tldr: The paper revises the Unified Colored-Noise Approximation (UCNA) for stochastic systems with colored noise, addressing critical issues in the original derivation, providing next-to-leading order corrections via a time-scale separation approach, and validating the framework on quartic potential and logistic growth examples.
AI.motivation: To identify and resolve critical issues in the original UCNA derivation for colored-noise stochastic dynamics, and to establish clearer limits of validity for approximations in both short and long correlation time regimes.
AI.method: A time-scale separation procedure is used to recast the UCNA framework, deriving next-to-leading order corrections for both vanishing and infinite correlation time limits, and comparing with alternative approximation methods.
AI.result: Next-to-leading order corrections to the dynamics are derived in both limiting regimes; relevant physical scalings of these approximations are highlighted; the framework's validity limits are clarified relative to other approximation procedures.
AI.conclusion: The refined UCNA formulation better defines the regime of applicability for colored-noise approximations, demonstrated via a quartic potential and stochastic logistic growth with multiplicative noise.

title: NIMO: A Software Platform for Closed-Loop Materials Exploration with Diverse AI Algorithms
summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs), where artificial intelligence proposes subsequent experiments and robotic systems execute them, are rapidly becoming the vanguard of materials discovery. A critical bottleneck, however, lies in seamlessly bridging diverse AI algorithms tailored for specific exploration goals with the heterogeneous robotic hardware found across different laboratories. Here, we present NIMO, an open-source software platform designed to dissolve this barrier through three core paradigms: a modular AI-robot decoupling mediated via simple CSV file exchange, a discrete candidate-pool architecture that seamlessly absorbs domain knowledge, and a unified Python interface pre-loaded with twelve distinct AI algorithms. In this Perspective, we review the operational principles of each algorithm alongside six diverse SDL implementations driven by NIMO, covering electrolyte discovery, organic synthesis, thin-film exploration, fuel-cell process informatics, coffee-ring phase exploration, and legacy liquid-handling automation. One of these also demonstrates NIMO's seamless interoperability with the IvoryOS orchestration framework. To democratize autonomous science, we also introduce a no-code desktop application that enables intuitive, human-in-the-loop exploration for non-programmers. NIMO is freely available at https://github.com/NIMS-DA/nimo, offering a versatile, plug-and-play foundation to accelerate autonomous materials exploration across diverse experimental landscapes.

AI.tldr: NIMO is an open-source software platform that bridges AI algorithms and robotic hardware for self-driving laboratories, featuring modular AI-robot decoupling, a candidate-pool architecture, 12 built-in AI algorithms, and a no-code interface, demonstrated across six diverse experimental domains.
AI.motivation: The critical bottleneck in self-driving laboratories is the lack of seamless integration between diverse AI exploration algorithms and heterogeneous robotic hardware across different labs.
AI.method: NIMO employs three core paradigms: (1) modular AI-robot decoupling via CSV file exchange, (2) a discrete candidate-pool architecture for incorporating domain knowledge, and (3) a unified Python interface with 12 pre-loaded AI algorithms, plus a no-code desktop application for non-programmers.
AI.result: NIMO has been demonstrated across six diverse SDL implementations: electrolyte discovery, organic synthesis, thin-film exploration, fuel-cell process informatics, coffee-ring phase exploration, and legacy liquid-handling automation, including interoperability with the IvoryOS framework.
AI.conclusion: NIMO offers a versatile, plug-and-play open-source foundation to democratize and accelerate autonomous materials exploration across diverse experimental landscapes.

title: Contacts to Low-Dimensional Semiconductors: Physical Theory and Analytical Model
summary: Metal contacts to low-dimensional semiconductors are critical for nanoelectronics, yet a general physical description has remained elusive. We present an analytical model for metal-induced gap states (MIGS), revealing a universal scaling law governed by semiconductor dimensionality. Linking MIGS to transport observables, we provide a unified formulation of Schottky barrier height, transfer length, and contact resistance. Our model explains recent experiments on carbon nanotubes and 2D materials, clarifying the fundamental criteria for achieving scalable, low-resistance contacts.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an analytical model for metal-induced gap states (MIGS) that reveals a universal scaling law governed by semiconductor dimensionality, linking MIGS to transport observables to provide a unified formulation of Schottky barrier height, transfer length, and contact resistance. The model explains recent experiments on carbon nanotubes and 2D materials, clarifying criteria for scalable, low-resistance contacts.
AI.motivation: Metal contacts to low-dimensional semiconductors are critical for nanoelectronics, yet a general physical description has remained elusive.
AI.method: The authors develop an analytical model for metal-induced gap states (MIGS) that reveals a universal scaling law governed by the dimensionality of the semiconductor. They link MIGS to key transport observables to formulate a unified description.
AI.result: The model provides a unified formulation of Schottky barrier height, transfer length, and contact resistance, and explains recent experimental results on carbon nanotubes and 2D materials.
AI.conclusion: The work clarifies the fundamental criteria for achieving scalable, low-resistance contacts to low-dimensional semiconductors.

title: Field-selected seven-site topological magnons in a classical frustrated triangular-lattice K-$Γ$-$Γ'$ magnet
summary: Defining magnon topology in strongly frustrated magnets is often hindered by the absence of a simple harmonic magnon vacuum at zero field. Within a classical-spin ground-state search followed by linear spin-wave theory (LSWT), we demonstrate that a representative triangular-lattice K-Gamma-Gamma' model in a dominant-Gamma exchange regime has an in-plane-field-selected compact, noncoplanar seven-site order. This field-selected state provides a controlled classical reference state and hosts magnon bands with field-tunable Chern numbers. Increasing the field drives a Dirac-like band touching that transfers Berry curvature between the fifth and sixth bands, altering the Chern vector from (0, 1, 0, -2, 1, 0, 0) to (0, 1, 0, -2, -1, 2, 0). This topological transition reorganizes the band-resolved thermal Hall conductivity, driving the total $κ_{xy}(T)$ through a near-zero crossing once the upper bands are thermally populated. The dynamical structure factor places roughly half of the coherent spectral weight on the Chern-active branches, offering a spectroscopic route to identify the topological branches. These results define a controlled semiclassical benchmark for magnon topology in this pure nearest-neighbor exchange model.

AI.tldr: This paper studies magnon topology in a frustrated triangular-lattice K-Gamma-Gamma' model under an in-plane magnetic field. Using classical ground-state search and linear spin-wave theory, the authors identify a field-induced noncoplanar seven-site order that supports magnon bands with tunable Chern numbers. A topological transition at higher fields changes the Chern vector and causes a near-zero crossing of the thermal Hall conductivity. The dynamical structure factor shows coherent spectral weight on Chern-active bands, enabling experimental identification.
AI.motivation: Magnon topology in strongly frustrated magnets is poorly understood because the harmonic magnon vacuum is undefined at zero field. This work aims to establish a controlled semiclassical reference for magnon topology in pure nearest-neighbor exchange models by studying a representative frustrated K-Gamma-Gamma' model under applied field.
AI.method: Classical-spin ground-state search followed by linear spin-wave theory (LSWT) applied to a triangular-lattice K-Gamma-Gamma' model in the dominant-Gamma exchange regime, with analysis of Chern numbers, thermal Hall conductivity, and dynamical structure factor.
AI.result: An in-plane field selects a compact, noncoplanar seven-site order. Magnon bands exhibit field-tunable Chern numbers; increasing field drives a Dirac-like band touching that changes the Chern vector from (0,1,0,-2,1,0,0) to (0,1,0,-2,-1,2,0). The total thermal Hall conductivity κ_xy(T) shows a near-zero crossing when upper bands are populated. About half of the coherent spectral weight resides on Chern-active branches.
AI.conclusion: The field-selected noncoplanar order provides a controlled classical reference state, defining a benchmark for magnon topology in this frustrated nearest-neighbor exchange model. The results offer a spectroscopic route to identify topological magnon branches.

title: Extracting Boundary Conformal Data from Periodic Non-Hermitian Critical Chains
summary: Boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) contains universal data that are usually accessed microscopically by imposing spatial boundaries on the lattice. Here, we introduce a periodic-chain projected-partition-function spectroscopy that extracts universal boundary quantities directly from non-Hermitian bulk-critical quantum chains, avoiding the need to engineer microscopic open boundaries and circumventing subtle boundary effects in non-Hermitian systems. Using a short-range-entangled boundary preparation and its infrared-compatible left dual, we obtain the Affleck-Ludwig boundary entropy in non-Hermitian systems. We demonstrate this construction for two representative non-Hermitian infrared structures. For a $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric Ising realization of the real nonunitary Yang-Lee CFT, we extract the minimal-boundary projected coefficient and recover a nontrivial negative excited-to-ground ratio. For the genuinely complex fixed points of the non-Hermitian five-state Potts chain, we resolve intrinsically complex boundary coefficients and reproduce the exact relation required by the Kramers-Wannier duality. Our results establish a route to nonunitary BCFT universal data via only knowledge of the bulk critical system, opening a window into non-Hermitian boundary criticality.

AI.tldr: The authors develop a "projected-partition-function spectroscopy" method that extracts boundary conformal field theory (BCFT) data, such as Affleck-Ludwig boundary entropy, from non-Hermitian bulk-critical quantum chains without requiring explicit open boundaries. The method is demonstrated on the PT-symmetric Yang-Lee CFT and the non-Hermitian five-state Potts chain, recovering nontrivial boundary coefficients and duality relations.
AI.motivation: Standard approaches to BCFT require imposing spatial boundaries on the lattice, which is problematic in non-Hermitian systems due to subtle boundary effects and the lack of a straightforward microscopic open-boundary construction. The authors aim to extract universal boundary data directly from bulk-critical non-Hermitian chains without engineering explicit boundaries.
AI.method: The method uses a periodic chain with a "projected-partition-function spectroscopy": a short-range-entangled boundary preparation and its infrared-compatible left dual are used to extract boundary quantities from the non-Hermitian bulk system. The construction avoids microscopic open boundaries by leveraging the non-Hermitian bulk criticality and its dual structure.
AI.result: For the PT-symmetric Ising realization of the real nonunitary Yang-Lee CFT, the minimal-boundary projected coefficient is extracted and a nontrivial negative excited-to-ground ratio is recovered. For the genuinely complex fixed points of the non-Hermitian five-state Potts chain, intrinsically complex boundary coefficients are resolved, and the exact relation required by Kramers-Wannier duality is reproduced.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a route to nonunitary BCFT universal data using only knowledge of the bulk critical system, opening a window into non-Hermitian boundary criticality and bypassing the need for explicit open-boundary engineering.

title: Switching Chern number by sliding and gating in alternately twisted tetralayer MoTe2
summary: Switching the bulk Chern number in topological materials is of central importance for the design of topological electronic devices. Motivated by recent observations of integer and fractional quantum anomalous Hall effects in twisted transition metal dichalcogenides (tTMDs), we realize the switching of valley Chern number through sliding and gating in alternately twisted tetralayer (ATT) MoTe$_{2}$. Using large-scale density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we show that the Chern number of the first $K$-valley moiré band evolves from $+1$ to $-1$ under the interlayer sliding. Furthermore, an applied electric field can switch the valley Chern number from $-1$ to $+1$. Based on the developed continuum model, we reveal that these switching behaviors are caused by the sliding- and gate-dependent intralayer moiré potential distributions across the layers. Our results establish ATT MoTe$_{2}$ as a promising platform for engineering moiré band topologies through the design of moiré potentials with sliding in multilayer moiré systems.

AI.tldr: Switching valley Chern number in alternately twisted tetralayer MoTe₂ via interlayer sliding and electric gating, enabling topological band engineering in multilayer moiré systems.
AI.motivation: Design of topological electronic devices requires switching the bulk Chern number; recent observations of quantum anomalous Hall effects in twisted TMDs motivate exploring Chern number control in multilayer moiré systems.
AI.method: Large-scale density functional theory (DFT) calculations and a continuum model to study sliding- and gate-dependent moiré potential distributions in alternately twisted tetralayer MoTe₂.
AI.result: The valley Chern number of the first K-valley moiré band switches from +1 to -1 under interlayer sliding, and from -1 to +1 under an applied electric field.
AI.conclusion: ATT MoTe₂ is a promising platform for engineering moiré band topologies via sliding-controlled moiré potentials in multilayer moiré systems.

title: Hidden chirality and half-vortex formation in exciton-polariton condensates
summary: We show that a radially symmetric, nonresonantly pumped spinor exciton-polariton condensate can acquire chirality without a rotating drive, chiral geometry, or pump orbital angular momentum. Spin relaxation in a two-reservoir system shifts the reservoir-induced blueshift relative to the gain profile, creating an effective non-Hermitian chiral potential. A reduced angular-mode theory reveals tunable exceptional points and non-reciprocal coupling between counter-rotating modes. Full driven-dissipative Gross-Pitaevskii simulations show that this hidden chirality enables all-optical formation of spin-selective half-vortices.

AI.tldr: Spinor exciton-polariton condensates can spontaneously acquire chirality without rotating drives or chiral geometry, through spin relaxation in a two-reservoir system that creates a non-Hermitian chiral potential, enabling all-optical formation of spin-selective half-vortices.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that chirality can emerge in a radially symmetric, nonresonantly pumped spinor exciton-polariton condensate without external rotating drives, chiral geometry, or pump orbital angular momentum.
AI.method: Theoretical analysis using a reduced angular-mode theory to reveal exceptional points and non-reciprocal coupling, combined with full driven-dissipative Gross-Pitaevskii simulations.
AI.result: Spin relaxation in a two-reservoir system shifts the reservoir-induced blueshift relative to the gain profile, creating an effective non-Hermitian chiral potential that leads to tunable exceptional points and non-reciprocal coupling between counter-rotating modes.
AI.conclusion: This hidden chirality enables all-optical formation of spin-selective half-vortices without requiring any rotating drive, chiral geometry, or pump orbital angular momentum.

title: Spin-orbit-entangled $J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2}$ magnetism and unconventional spin freezing in the bond-disordered pyrochlore antiferromagnet NaCdCo$_2$F$_7$
summary: Bond disorder in frustrated pyrochlore antiferromagnets can give rise to fundamentally different quantum ground states depending on the nature of the local magnetic moments. Here, we show that the bond-disordered pyrochlore NaCdCo$_2$F$_7$ realizes an unconventional spin-glass-like state with continued dynamics, in stark contrast to its isostructural $S=\frac{1}{2}$ NaCdCu$_2$F$_7$ counterpart. High-field magnetization and Co $L_{2,3}$-edge XAS/XMCD establish spin-orbit-entangled $J_{\rm eff}=\frac{1}{2}$ Co$^{2+}$ moments with a substantial unquenched orbital contribution, consistent with local $XY$ anisotropy seen in the isostructural Na$A''$Co$_2$F$_7$ ($A''$ = Ca, Sr) analogues. $μ$SR and $^{23}$Na NMR measurements reveal progressive slowing of spin fluctuations below $\sim10$ K, culminating in a partially frozen state with persistent low-temperature dynamics that deviates from a canonical spin glass. Comparison with the isostructural bond-disordered pyrochlore NaCdCu$_2$F$_7$, which realizes a random-singlet state, reveals a fundamentally different response of spin-orbit-entangled Co$^{2+}$ moments to bond disorder. These results identify spin-orbit coupling as a key ingredient governing the fate of bond-disordered frustrated pyrochlore magnets.

AI.tldr: Bond-disordered pyrochlore NaCdCo₂F₇ exhibits a spin-glass-like state with persistent dynamics due to spin-orbit-entangled Co²⁺ moments, unlike the random-singlet state in its S=1/2 Cu²⁺ counterpart, highlighting spin-orbit coupling as a key factor in bond-disordered frustrated magnets.
AI.motivation: To understand how bond disorder in frustrated pyrochlore antiferromagnets leads to fundamentally different quantum ground states depending on the nature of local magnetic moments, specifically the role of spin-orbit coupling.
AI.method: High-field magnetization, Co L₂,₃-edge XAS/XMCD, μSR, and ²³Na NMR measurements on NaCdCo₂F₇, compared with isostructural NaCdCu₂F₇ and NaA''Co₂F₇ (A'' = Ca, Sr) analogues.
AI.result: NaCdCo₂F₇ hosts J_eff=1/2 Co²⁺ moments with substantial unquenched orbital contribution, consistent with local XY anisotropy. Below ~10 K, progressive slowing of spin fluctuations leads to a partially frozen state with persistent low-temperature dynamics, deviating from canonical spin-glass behavior. This contrasts with the random-singlet state in NaCdCu₂F₇.
AI.conclusion: Spin-orbit coupling is a key ingredient governing the fate of bond-disordered frustrated pyrochlore magnets, as spin-orbit-entangled Co²⁺ moments respond fundamentally differently to bond disorder compared to S=1/2 Cu²⁺ moments.

title: Riviera model with egoistical settlers
summary: The Riviera model mimics a densifying settlement along the coastline. In the lattice version, houses are built sequentially in empty sites with the constraint that every newly built house has at least one empty neighboring site. The distribution of clusters of adjacent houses does not obey a closed set of evolutionary equations, but the void-cluster-void distribution does. We compute the latter and extract the cluster distribution from it. In the jammed state, when all voids have length one and the evolution ceases, the cluster distribution has a neat form and exhibits a factorial decay with the length of the cluster. To investigate finite systems, we employ a static approach directly treating jammed states. If the coastline is a finite segment, we determine the statistics of the number of empty sites in the jammed state (the average, variance, and higher cumulants). We also study a continuum version in which houses are built along the line so that each newly built house is sufficiently separated from at least one neighboring house.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes the Riviera model, a sequential settlement process where houses are built along a coastline with the constraint that each new house must have an empty neighbor. It derives cluster distributions using void-cluster-void statistics, finds factorial decay in jammed states, and studies both lattice and continuum versions for finite systems.
AI.motivation: To understand the statistical properties of densifying settlements along a coastline, specifically the distribution of clusters of adjacent houses in both lattice and continuum models under a nearest-neighbor emptiness constraint.
AI.method: The authors analyze the lattice Riviera model by computing void-cluster-void distributions (which obey closed evolutionary equations) and extracting cluster distributions from them. For finite systems, they use a static approach focusing on jammed states. They also study a continuum version.
AI.result: In the jammed state (where all voids have length one), the cluster distribution exhibits factorial decay with cluster length. For finite coastline segments, the statistics (average, variance, higher cumulants) of empty sites in the jammed state are determined.
AI.conclusion: The void-cluster-void distribution provides a tractable way to analyze the Riviera model. The jammed state yields neat factorial decay, and both lattice and continuum versions are amenable to exact statistical analysis.

title: Carbon Layer Orientation and Closed-Pore Construction Achieving Ultra-Low Specific Surface Area Hard Carbon for High-Performance Na-ion Storage
summary: Addressing the critical trade-off between initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE) and reversible capacity in hard carbon anodes for Na-ion batteries (NIBs), we introduce a novel coupling strategy that combines carbon layer orientation reconstruction with closed-pore construction to produce hard carbon with an ultra-low specific surface area. We demonstrate that the nanographite domains within the hard carbon precursor undergo entropy-driven orientation reconstruction through the synergistic regulation of heteroatom doping and medium-temperature carbonization. This process not only increases interlayer spacing and promotes structural disorder but also enables the formation of dense, closed pores and ultramicropores at domain boundaries via confined atomic migration, while simultaneously encapsulating surface open pores within internal closed ones. Due to this unique pore architecture, our hard carbon exhibits an ultra-low specific surface area of 1.89 m2 g-1 with a markedly higher proportion of closed pores. As a result, our hard carbon achieves a remarkable reversible capacity of 342.3 mAh g-1 at 20 mA g-1, with an exceptional ICE of 90.4% and a dominant plateau capacity of 262.3 mAh g-1 (76.6%) for NIBs. We believe this coupling strategy provides a new paradigm for the structural engineering of high-ICE anode materials in advanced NIBs.

AI.tldr: A coupling strategy of carbon layer orientation reconstruction and closed-pore construction produces hard carbon with ultra-low surface area (1.89 m² g⁻¹), achieving high reversible capacity (342.3 mAh g⁻¹), exceptional ICE (90.4%), and dominant plateau capacity (262.3 mAh g⁻¹) for Na-ion batteries.
AI.motivation: To address the critical trade-off between initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE) and reversible capacity in hard carbon anodes for Na-ion batteries.
AI.method: A coupling strategy combining carbon layer orientation reconstruction (via entropy-driven process through heteroatom doping and medium-temperature carbonization) with closed-pore construction to produce hard carbon with ultra-low specific surface area.
AI.result: Ultra-low specific surface area of 1.89 m² g⁻¹, high proportion of closed pores, reversible capacity of 342.3 mAh g⁻¹ at 20 mA g⁻¹, ICE of 90.4%, and dominant plateau capacity of 262.3 mAh g⁻¹ (76.6%).
AI.conclusion: This coupling strategy provides a new paradigm for structural engineering of high-ICE anode materials in advanced Na-ion batteries.

title: Unveiling AlSb as a Promising Zincblende Semiconductor for Visible-Light Shift-Current Generation
summary: We use density functional theory to investigate the shift-current response in zincblende III--V (AlP, AlAs, AlSb, GaP, GaAs, InP, InAs, and InSb) and II--VI (ZnS, ZnSe, ZnTe, CdS, CdSe, and CdTe) semiconductors. Our main goal is to identify which material generates the largest shift-current under illumination and to examine the factors influencing this response. We find that aluminum-containing semiconductors, particularly AlSb, exhibit the highest shift-current responses, while CdSe shows the lowest. We analyze the contributions of specific band-to-band transitions to the shift-current in AlSb by selectively summing valence and conduction bands. Additionally, we calculate delocalization indices to investigate the electron delocalization, which correlates with the shift current. Hydrostatic pressure does not enhance the shift current in these materials. These findings have potential applications in optoelectronics and identify the most promising zincblende semiconductors for efficient shift-current generation under visible-light illumination

AI.tldr: DFT study of shift-current response in III-V and II-VI zincblende semiconductors finds AlSb exhibits the highest shift-current, CdSe the lowest, with hydrostatic pressure not enhancing the response.
AI.motivation: To identify which zincblende semiconductor generates the largest shift-current under illumination and to understand the factors influencing this response.
AI.method: Density functional theory (DFT) calculations of shift-current response; band-to-band transition analysis using selective summation of valence and conduction bands; calculation of delocalization indices to study electron delocalization; hydrostatic pressure effects examined.
AI.result: Aluminum-containing semiconductors (especially AlSb) show highest shift-current responses; CdSe shows the lowest. Hydrostatic pressure does not enhance shift current.
AI.conclusion: AlSb is identified as the most promising zincblende semiconductor for efficient shift-current generation under visible-light illumination, with potential optoelectronic applications.

title: Direct Nanoscale Pyroelectric Characterization of a CuInP${}_2$S${}_6$ van der Waals Nanogenerator
summary: Pyroelectric energy conversion offers a route for harvesting time-dependent thermalfluctuations that are abundant in natural and technological environments. Twodimensional ferroelectrics are particularly attractive for this purpose because reduced dimensionality enables ultrathin, mechanically compliant device architectures. Here, we demonstrate direct nanoscale pyroelectric characterization of an out-of-plane van der Waals nanogenerator based on CuInP2S6 (CIPS) encapsulated between few-layer graphene electrodes. A scanning thermal microscopy (SThM) probe is employed as a localized nanoscale heat source while the electrically generated response is measured in situ through the device electrodes. Harmonic detection isolates the pyroelectric signal from parasitic first-harmonic electromechanical contributions, while finite-element thermal modeling combined with probe calibration enables direct determination of the local pyroelectric coefficient from the measured electrical response. Beyond quantitative characterization, the spatially resolved measurements directly identify electrically inactive regions associated with device defects, revealing local performance-limiting features that remain hidden in conventional spatially averaged pyroelectric measurements. The presented approach establishes a versatile platform for quantitative nanoscale pyroelectric characterization and the optimization of van der Waals pyroelectric devices.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates nanoscale pyroelectric characterization of a CuInP2S6 van der Waals nanogenerator using scanning thermal microscopy with harmonic detection and finite-element modeling, enabling quantitative local pyroelectric coefficient measurement and identification of electrically inactive defect regions.
AI.motivation: Pyroelectric energy conversion can harvest time-dependent thermal fluctuations, and two-dimensional ferroelectrics offer advantages of ultrathin, mechanically compliant devices for this purpose, but nanoscale characterization methods are needed.
AI.method: A scanning thermal microscopy probe serves as a localized nanoscale heat source on a CIPS nanogenerator encapsulated between few-layer graphene electrodes. Harmonic detection isolates the pyroelectric signal from first-harmonic electromechanical contributions, and finite-element thermal modeling with probe calibration determines the local pyroelectric coefficient from the measured electrical response.
AI.result: Spatially resolved measurements directly identify electrically inactive regions associated with device defects, revealing local performance-limiting features hidden in conventional spatially averaged pyroelectric measurements.
AI.conclusion: The approach establishes a versatile platform for quantitative nanoscale pyroelectric characterization and optimization of van der Waals pyroelectric devices.

title: Electronic Green's function across the pseudogap to stripe transition in the $t$-$t'$-$J$ model
summary: Superconducting domes in strongly correlated electronic systems are often accompanied by charge density waves and peculiar features in the electronic structure. The appearance of a pseudogap, in particular, and its relation to charge density waves remains insufficiently understood. Here, we investigate the electronic Green's function of the underdoped $t$-$t'$-$J$ model of the cuprate superconductors using tensor network algorithms for finite temperature dynamics on cylinders of width $4$. We find the prominent momentum differentiation, the hallmark of the pseudogap, to be strongly dependent on $t'$, which develops into a momentum-dependent opening of a gap upon decreasing temperature, consistent with the formation of a Fermi arc at intermediate temperatures. The nodal gap around ${\bf k}=(π/2,π/2)$ closes and fills with increasing temperature as coherent stripe order melts into a regime of fluctuating charge clusters.

AI.tldr: Using tensor network algorithms, the authors study the t-t'-J model of cuprate superconductors and find that the pseudogap phenomenon—characterized by momentum-dependent gap opening and Fermi arc formation—is strongly dependent on the t' parameter and arises from fluctuating charge clusters as stripe order melts with increasing temperature.
AI.motivation: To understand the relationship between the pseudogap and charge density waves in strongly correlated electronic systems like cuprate superconductors, which remains insufficiently understood.
AI.method: Tensor network algorithms for finite temperature dynamics applied to the underdoped t-t'-J model on width-4 cylinders.
AI.result: The pseudogap's momentum differentiation is strongly dependent on t'; a momentum-dependent gap opens with decreasing temperature, forming a Fermi arc at intermediate temperatures; the nodal gap near k=(π/2,π/2) closes and fills with increasing temperature as coherent stripe order melts into fluctuating charge clusters.
AI.conclusion: The pseudogap in cuprate superconductors is intimately connected to fluctuating charge clusters arising from the melting of stripe order, with the t' parameter playing a crucial role in the momentum-dependent gap structure.

title: Exact solution of the Glauber-Ising model on the finite-length semi-open chain
summary: The exact time-space correlation function of the $1D$ Glauber-Ising model, quenched to temperature $T=0$ and on a semi-open lattice of finite size $N$, is obtained. This also allows to deduce the exact empty-interval probability of the dual $1D$ coagulation-diffusion process on a periodic finite ring and to reproduce the long-time decay of the particle concentration. These results are consistent with the generic expectations of dynamical finite-size scaling theory.

AI.tldr: The paper derives the exact time-space correlation function for the 1D Glauber-Ising model quenched to T=0 on a semi-open finite lattice, uses it to compute the empty-interval probability for the dual coagulation-diffusion process on a periodic ring, and confirms dynamical finite-size scaling predictions.
AI.motivation: To obtain exact analytic results for non-equilibrium dynamics in finite-size systems, particularly the time-space correlation function of the Glauber-Ising model at zero temperature, which serves as a testing ground for dynamical finite-size scaling theory.
AI.method: Analytical solution of the exact time-space correlation function for the 1D Glauber-Ising model on a semi-open lattice of finite size N quenched to T=0; deduction of the empty-interval probability for the dual coagulation-diffusion process on a periodic finite ring.
AI.result: Exact expression for the time-space correlation function; exact empty-interval probability for the dual process; reproduction of the long-time decay of particle concentration; consistency with dynamical finite-size scaling theory.
AI.conclusion: The results validate the generic expectations of dynamical finite-size scaling theory through exact solutions in a finite-size, non-equilibrium setting.

title: Dimensional Crossover of Mass Anisotropy in Ta-doped WTe2
summary: The observation of extremely large magnetoresistance in WTe2 has attracted considerable attention towards understanding its underlying origin. With its layered van der Waals structure, the question that remains largely unexplored is whether the three-dimensional anisotropic transport characteristics of WTe2 persists under chemical substitution. Here, we present a systematic angle-dependent magneto-transport study of single-crystalline TaxW1-xTe2 (x = 0, 0.05, 0.1). The results are analysed within a mass anisotropy scaling framework to extract the mass anisotropy parameter γ as a function of temperature and doping. It is observed that Ta substitution leads to monotonic increase of γ across all temperatures, indicating a progressive deepening of quasi-two-dimensional Fermi surface character. Ta doping also leads to a substantial improvement in crystalline quality, reflected in a pronounced increase in the residual resistivity ratio. Despite weakening electron-hole compensation, the magnetoresistance rises sharply to ~58,211% at x = 0.1, which is assigned to a substantial enhancement in carrier mobility. Rietveld refinement confirms a systematic c-axis contraction with Ta content, identifying the structural origin of the enhanced anisotropy. The mass anisotropy scaling that holds for x = 0 and x = 0.05 breaks down for x = 0.1, where the angular magneto-resistance anisotropy substantially exceeds single-ellipsoid predictions, pointing to a multi-pocket Fermi surface with distinct anisotropies. Nonlinear Hall resistivity provides independent evidence for the underlying multiband character of transport in this system. These findings demonstrate that Fermi surface anisotropy, carrier compensation, and mobility are independent parameters that can lead to tuneable control of large magnetoresistance in topological semimetal WTe2.

AI.tldr: This study investigates angle-dependent magneto-transport in Ta-substituted WTe2 (TaxW1-xTe2, x=0, 0.05, 0.1), finding that Ta doping increases mass anisotropy γ, improves crystalline quality, and boosts magnetoresistance to ~58,211% at x=0.1 despite weakened electron-hole compensation, primarily due to enhanced carrier mobility. The mass anisotropy scaling breaks down at x=0.1, indicating a multi-pocket Fermi surface, and the c-axis contraction from doping structurally drives the enhanced anisotropy.
AI.motivation: To explore whether the 3D anisotropic transport characteristics of WTe2 persist under chemical substitution (Ta doping), and to understand the tunability of large magnetoresistance via Fermi surface anisotropy, carrier compensation, and mobility.
AI.method: Systematic angle-dependent magneto-transport measurements on single-crystalline TaxW1-xTe2 (x=0, 0.05, 0.1), analyzed using a mass anisotropy scaling framework, complemented by Rietveld refinement of structural parameters and Hall resistivity measurements.
AI.result: Ta substitution monotonically increases mass anisotropy γ across all temperatures, deepens quasi-2D Fermi surface character, improves crystalline quality (higher RRR), and enhances magnetoresistance to ~58,211% at x=0.1 despite weaker electron-hole compensation, due to mobility enhancement. Rietveld refinement shows systematic c-axis contraction. Mass anisotropy scaling holds for x=0 and 0.05 but breaks at x=0.1, indicating multi-pocket Fermi surface. Nonlinear Hall resistivity confirms multiband transport.
AI.conclusion: Fermi surface anisotropy, carrier compensation, and mobility are independent parameters enabling tunable control of large magnetoresistance in topological semimetal WTe2 via chemical substitution.

title: Real-space spectral functions of three-dimensional billion-size topological non-Hermitian matter with tensor networks
summary: Non-Hermitian systems host a wide range of unconventional topological phenomena while large-scale simulations in finite three dimensional systems remain challenging because of the rapidly growing number of sites. In particular, higher-order topological corner modes are often studied only in small lattices, where strong finite-size effects can mask their intrinsic behavior. Here, we develop a tensor-network framework that combines quantics tensor cross interpolation with the kernel polynomial method, enabling compact representations of large non-Hermitian tight-binding Hamiltonians and direct calculations of real-space spectral functions for systems exceeding one billion lattice sites. Using this approach, we investigate three-dimensional non-Hermitian higher-order topological insulators with with structured real-space geometries. The unprecedented system size enables direct access to the macroscopic regime and allows corner-mode spectral responses to be resolved in genuinely three-dimensional systems.By tuning the loss strength, we identify distinct in-gap corner modes across weak- and strong-loss regimes.Our results establish tensor-network algorithms as a powerful strategy to perform real-space spectral calculations in exceptionally large non-Hermitian systems.
